# Inertia.Net documentation

> Inertia.Net is a .NET 10 and .NET 11 server adapter for Inertia.js v3. ASP.NET Core endpoints (Minimal APIs, MVC or FastEndpoints) return a page component name and props; React, Vue or Svelte renders them. There is no separate JSON API or client-side router.

---

# Introduction

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/introduction

> Inertia.Net is a .NET 10 and .NET 11 server adapter for Inertia.js v3. Build React, Vue and Svelte apps without a separate API.

Inertia.Net lets your C# routes render React, Vue or Svelte pages. In each route, you choose a component and pass it the data it needs. Inertia calls that data **props**. Sign-in, validation and database queries live in your ASP.NET Core app. Your frontend framework handles what the user sees and interacts with.

You can build and ship the server and frontend as one app. Start with a working todo app and try a C# validation rule in the browser. [First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes)

## How it works

<Steps>
  <Step title="An endpoint chooses a page and its props">

```csharp
app.MapGet("/", () => Render("Home", new InertiaProps
{
    ["greeting"] = "Hello from .NET",
}));
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Inertia connects it to a client component">

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
export default function Home({ greeting }: { greeting: string }) {
  return <h1>{greeting}</h1>
}
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
defineProps<{ greeting: string }>()
</script>

<template>
  <h1>{{ greeting }}</h1>
</template>
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  let { greeting }: { greeting: string } = $props()
</script>

<h1>{greeting}</h1>
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

  </Step>
  <Step title="The client updates the page">
    The first request returns HTML with the page object embedded. The page object holds the component name and its props. Inertia links and form submissions request the next page in the background and swap the component while the browser keeps its state.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Your .NET app still handles the request. The adapter adds the protocol middleware, prop resolution, redirect semantics, flash data and asset tags.

## What you get

<Cards>
  <Card title="Three backend styles" icon="server" href="/docs/quick-start">
    Minimal APIs, MVC controllers and FastEndpoints share the same core package and protocol behavior.
  </Card>
  <Card title="The full v3 prop model" icon="blocks" href="/docs/props">
    Lazy, optional, deferred, merged, once, cached, rescued and infinite-scroll props.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Production concerns included" icon="shield" href="/docs/csrf-and-antiforgery">
    CSRF cookies, encrypted state, asset versioning, proxy support and SSR supervision.
  </Card>
  <Card title="AOT-friendly by design" icon="rocket" href="/docs/native-aot">
    Props are written through System.Text.Json metadata. Inertia.Net does not use reflection over your page objects.
  </Card>
</Cards>

## Feature matrix

| | Minimal API | MVC controllers | FastEndpoints |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Package | `Inertia.Net` | `Inertia.Net` + `Inertia.Net.Mvc` | `Inertia.Net` + `Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints` |
| Render / Back / Location | `Render(...)` returns `IResult` | same, return `IResult` from an action | `Send.InertiaAsync(...)` or return the result |
| Validation redirect with errors | `.WithInertiaValidation()` | `ModelState` filter (global) | `c.ConfigureInertia()` pre-processor |
| Precognition | `.WithInertiaPrecognition()` | not available | `c.ConfigureInertia()` |
| Razor root view | no (`app.html` template) | optional (tag helpers) | no (`app.html` template) |
| Native AOT | yes | no (MVC itself is not AOT) | yes (with the FastEndpoints source generator) |

The client packages are `@inertiajs/react`, `@inertiajs/vue3` and `@inertiajs/svelte`, all version 3. Inertia.Net does not support v2 clients.

## This documentation site

This site is an Inertia.Net app. The sidebar, search, docs pages and theme switcher are React components rendered by an ASP.NET Core Minimal API. Navigation uses Inertia links. The source is in `docs/Inertia.Net.Docs`, so the site is also a real example.

## Requirements

- .NET 10 or .NET 11 SDK
- JavaScript frontend build tools with npm, Bun, pnpm or Yarn. Managed SSR requires Node.js or Bun at runtime
- An Inertia.js v3 client package for React, Vue or Svelte

<Callout type="tip" title="Starting from scratch?">
Use the starter template: `dotnet new install Inertia.Net.Templates`, then `dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react`. It includes working pages, a form with validation, flash messages, CSRF and Vite configuration.
</Callout>

- [Why Inertia?](/docs/why-inertia) explains what you get with C# on the server and React, Vue or Svelte in the browser.
- [First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes) takes you from the template to a working form you can change.
- [Install the packages](/docs/installation) in an existing app.
- [Follow the quick start](/docs/quick-start) for a minimal end-to-end setup.
- [Read the props reference](/docs/props) when you are ready to model page data.

# Why Inertia?

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/why-inertia

> Build a C# backend for React, Vue or Svelte and see what Inertia.Net handles between them.

## Coming from TypeScript?

Keep React, Vue or Svelte and the frontend tools you know. Write your routes and business logic in C#. The compiler checks your server code at build time. You can set a breakpoint in a C# route and step through it as you click around the app.

ASP.NET Core gives you routing, cookie sign-in and authorization in one web framework. When you add a database, Entity Framework Core lets you write queries in C# and manage schema changes alongside the app.

Inertia.Net can generate TypeScript types from your C# page data and named routes. Change a field in C# and your editor can show where the frontend needs to change. [TypeScript types](/docs/typescript) · [Typed routes](/docs/typed-routes)

## Already building in .NET?

Keep your ASP.NET Core routes, controllers and validation rules. Add interactive pages in React, Vue or Svelte in the same project. The starter shows the whole workflow with a todo form. A C# rule checks the title, and Inertia makes the error available beside the input. [First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes)

## From a C# route to a page

Your C# handler chooses a frontend component and supplies its data. This route sends a list of users to the `Users/Index` page.

```csharp
app.MapGet("/users", (UserStore users) =>
    Render("Users/Index", new InertiaProps { ["users"] = users.All() }));
```

The matching component receives `users` as a prop, the same way it receives data passed in by another component.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
export default function Index({ users }: { users: { id: number; name: string }[] }) {
  return <ul>{users.map((u) => <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>)}</ul>
}
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
defineProps<{ users: { id: number; name: string }[] }>()
</script>

<template>
  <ul>
    <li v-for="u in users" :key="u.id">{{ u.name }}</li>
  </ul>
</template>
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  let { users }: { users: { id: number; name: string }[] } = $props()
</script>

<ul>
  {#each users as u (u.id)}
    <li>{u.name}</li>
  {/each}
</ul>
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

On the first visit, Inertia.Net sends HTML. When someone follows an Inertia link, the server sends the next page's data as JSON and the browser updates the screen without a full reload.

Inertia fits apps where the frontend and backend ship together, including dashboards, admin tools and SaaS products. If mobile apps or third parties also need access to your data, you can add API endpoints alongside your Inertia pages.

## How a request works

The Inertia client sends the `X-Inertia` header when it requests a page in the background. Inertia.Net uses that header to send the page as JSON.

<Sequence
  caption="A direct visit loads HTML. An Inertia link requests the next page as JSON."
  actors={[
    { name: 'Browser', sub: 'Inertia client' },
    { name: 'ASP.NET Core', sub: 'Inertia.Net' },
    { name: 'Your handler', sub: 'route or controller' },
  ]}
  messages={[
    { from: 0, to: 1, text: 'GET /users', code: 'Accept: text/html', phase: 'First visit' },
    { from: 1, to: 2, text: 'Run the route' },
    { from: 2, to: 1, text: 'Return the page name and props', reply: true, code: 'Render("Users/Index", props)' },
    { from: 1, to: 0, text: 'HTML with the page data embedded', reply: true, code: '<script data-page="app" type="application/json">' },
    { from: 0, to: 0, text: 'Client app boots and renders the page' },
    { from: 0, to: 1, text: 'Follow an Inertia link to /users/1', code: 'X-Inertia: true', phase: 'Inertia navigation' },
    { from: 1, to: 2, text: 'Run the route' },
    { from: 2, to: 1, text: 'Same Render call', reply: true },
    { from: 1, to: 0, text: 'Only the page object, as JSON', reply: true, code: '{ "component": "Users/Show", "props": {...} }' },
    { from: 0, to: 0, text: 'Swap the page component, no reload' },
  ]}
/>

## In more detail

### Inertia vs a SPA plus a Web API

| | SPA + Web API | Inertia.Net |
|---|---|---|
| Projects to build and deploy | A JSON API and a separate client app, often with different hosts and CORS rules | One ASP.NET Core app that also builds your frontend |
| Routing | A server router for the API and a client router for pages, kept in sync by hand | ASP.NET Core routes only. Each route renders a page |
| Data loading | Fetch calls, loading states and caching in each component | Props arrive with the page. Slow data can be [deferred](/docs/deferred-props) |
| Authentication | Tokens or cookies shared across two apps, plus client-side route guards | Your normal ASP.NET Core cookie auth and `[Authorize]` |
| Validation | Return an error shape from the API and map it to forms in the client | Redirect back with errors, available as `form.errors` ([validation](/docs/validation-and-errors)) |
| API contract | You design, version and document JSON endpoints | The props you pass are the contract. [TypeScript types](/docs/typescript) can be generated |
| Frontend | React, Vue or Svelte | React, Vue or Svelte |

You still write components, hooks and styles. What you no longer write is the connecting code: the API layer, the client router, and the code that keeps state in sync with the server.

### Features

| Area | What you get | Learn more |
|---|---|---|
| Backends | Minimal APIs, MVC controllers and FastEndpoints on one core package | [Quick start](/docs/quick-start) |
| Clients | React, Vue and Svelte with the Inertia.js v3 client | [Client setup](/docs/client-setup) |
| Shared data | Props sent with every page, such as the signed-in user, set statically or per request | [Shared data](/docs/shared-data) |
| Validation | Redirect back with errors before your handler runs, with named error bags | [Validation](/docs/validation-and-errors) |
| Precognition | Validate a form before it is submitted, without running the handler | [Precognition](/docs/precognition) |
| Flash data | One-time messages or typed values that survive a redirect | [Flash data](/docs/flash-data) |
| Redirects and history | `Back()`, `Location()`, external redirects, history encryption and clearing | [Redirects and history](/docs/redirects-and-history) |
| Error pages | Routing failures and unhandled exceptions rendered as Inertia pages | [Error pages](/docs/error-pages) |
| Asset versioning | The client reloads once when your JavaScript or CSS changes | [Asset versioning](/docs/asset-versioning) |
| Vite | Manifest and dev-server tags, CDN base URLs, prefetching and CSP nonces | [Vite](/docs/vite-integration) |
| Server-side rendering | Render the first visit on Node or Bun, supervised by the app, with a fallback to client rendering | [SSR](/docs/server-side-rendering) |
| CSRF | The `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie and `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header, configured for you | [CSRF](/docs/csrf-and-antiforgery) |
| Multiple apps | Mount a second Inertia UI under its own path with its own shared props and root view | [Mounts](/docs/mounts) |
| Native AOT | Minimal API apps publish as Native AOT, using source-generated JSON metadata | [Native AOT](/docs/native-aot) |
| TypeScript | Generate declarations for page props, shared props and flash data from .NET types | [TypeScript types](/docs/typescript) |
| Testing | Fluent assertions over Inertia responses, with helpers for partial reloads and deferred props | [Testing](/docs/testing) |
| DevTools | Record visits for the Inertia DevTools extension and catch missing page components | [DevTools](/docs/devtools) |

### Prop features

Props are the data a page receives. Most of Inertia's performance and user-experience features are choices about how a prop is sent.

| Prop type | In C# | What it does | Learn more |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain | `["title"] = "Hi"` | Sent on every response that includes the key | [Props](/docs/props) |
| Lazy | `Prop(() => ...)` | The loader runs only when the prop is part of the response | [Props](/docs/props) |
| Always | `Always(value)` | Sent even when a partial reload does not ask for it | [Partial reloads](/docs/partial-reloads) |
| Optional | `Optional(() => ...)` | Never sent on the first visit, only when a partial reload asks for it | [Partial reloads](/docs/partial-reloads) |
| Deferred | `Defer(() => ..., group: "stats")` | Left out of the first response, then loaded right away so the page shows up sooner | [Deferred props](/docs/deferred-props) |
| Merge | `Merge(value)`, `DeepMerge(value)` | The client appends or deep merges new data instead of replacing it | [Merging props](/docs/merging-props) |
| Once | `Once(() => ...)` | Resolved once and remembered by the client, with optional expiry | [Once props](/docs/once-props) |
| Infinite scroll | `Scroll(page, ...)` | Merges pages of items and reports paging metadata | [Infinite scroll](/docs/infinite-scroll) |
| Rescued | `.Rescue()` | If its loader throws, the prop is left out and reported in `rescuedProps` instead of failing the whole page | [Props](/docs/props) |
| Parallel | `.Parallel()` | Starts independent async loaders together instead of one after another | [Props](/docs/props) |
| Cached | `.Cache(key, duration)` | Caches a loader's result between requests | [Props](/docs/props) |
| Live | live props | Refresh themselves when the server broadcasts an event, over SignalR or your own transport | [Live props](/docs/live-props) |

Partial reloads let the client ask for only some props, with `only` and `except`. A filter change or a poll then does not recompute the whole page. See [Pagination](/docs/pagination) for the numbered and cursor pages that feed pagers and infinite scroll.

### When it is not a good fit

- **You need a public API anyway.** Mobile apps, third-party integrations or several different clients need real JSON endpoints. You can build those next to your Inertia pages, but Inertia will not replace them.
- **The frontend is a separate product.** If another team deploys the frontend on its own schedule, a versioned API is the cleaner boundary.
- **Heavy offline use.** Inertia expects the server for every page change.
- **You want no JavaScript at all.** For server-rendered HTML with a little interactivity, Razor Pages or Blazor may be simpler.

## Next steps

- [First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes) creates an app from the starter template and walks through a validated form.
- [Quick start](/docs/quick-start) adds Inertia.Net to an existing ASP.NET Core app.
- [Introduction](/docs/introduction) summarizes what the adapter provides.

# First 10 minutes

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/first-10-minutes

> Run your first app, change a C# validation rule, and see the result in your browser.

You'll run a small todo app, submit a form, and change how C# validates it. The starter sets up ASP.NET Core, your frontend, and Vite for you.

To see a complete app first, explore [Kitchen Sink](/docs/kitchen-sink), the official Inertia.js v3 sample app.
It uses Laravel and Vue. This guide runs the same server-driven page model on .NET.

## 1. Create the app

Install the [.NET 10 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/download/dotnet/10.0). The commands below also need Node.js 22.12 or newer with npm. To check what you have, run `dotnet --list-sdks` and look for a 10.0 SDK, then run `node --version` to see the Node version.

Run these commands in the folder where you want to create `MyApp`.

```sh
dotnet new install Inertia.Net.Templates@1.9.8
dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react
cd MyApp
npm install
npm run dev
```

For Vue or Svelte, use `--framework vue` or `--framework svelte` in the `dotnet new inertia` command. For .NET 11, install the .NET 11 SDK and add `--tfm net11.0`.

Leave Vite running. In a second terminal, open the same `MyApp` folder and start the server.

```sh
dotnet watch
```

Open [http://localhost:5180/todos](http://localhost:5180/todos) in your browser. That is the address `dotnet watch` prints. Vite also prints an address on port 5173. Vite uses that address to serve JavaScript, CSS and live updates to the page.

## 2. Change a C# validation rule

1. With the title empty, click **Add**. The page shows an error below the input.
2. In `Program.cs`, find `NewTodo` and change `StringLength(100)` to `StringLength(10)`. Save the file, then restart the server to load the new rule. To restart, press **Ctrl+C** in the server terminal and run `dotnet watch` again. Leave Vite running.
3. Enter `Buy groceries` and click **Add**. The new error shows the 10-character limit. Then try `Buy milk`. The todo appears in the list.

## 3. Follow the form from the browser to C#

In `Program.cs`, `MapPost` tells ASP.NET Core what to run when the browser submits to `/todos`. The name `todos.store` also gives the frontend a typed function for this route.

```csharp
app.MapPost("/todos", (HttpContext http, TodoStore todos, NewTodo input) =>
{
    todos.Add(input.Title!);
    http.Inertia().Flash("success", "Todo added");
    return Results.Redirect("/todos");
}).WithInertiaValidation().WithName("todos.store");
```

`WithInertiaValidation()` checks the rules on `NewTodo.Title`. If validation fails, Inertia.Net sends the browser back to the page with the error. If the title passes, the handler adds the todo and sends back a one-time success message.

Open the page file for your frontend: `ClientApp/pages/Todos/Index.tsx`, `Index.vue`, or `Index.svelte`. The excerpts below show how the form uses the generated route and displays `form.errors.title`.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
import { useForm } from '@inertiajs/react'
import type { FormEvent } from 'react'
import { routes } from '../../types/routes'

// Inside the page component:
const form = useForm({ title: '' })
const submit = (e: FormEvent) => {
  e.preventDefault()
  form.submit(routes.todos.store(), { onSuccess: () => form.reset() })
}

// Inside its return:
<form onSubmit={submit}>
  <input placeholder="What needs doing?" value={form.data.title} onChange={(e) => form.setData('title', e.target.value)} />
  <button type="submit" disabled={form.processing}>Add</button>
  {form.errors.title && <div style={{ color: 'crimson' }}>{form.errors.title}</div>}
</form>
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useForm } from '@inertiajs/vue3'
import { routes } from '../../types/routes'

const form = useForm({ title: '' })
const submit = () => form.submit(routes.todos.store(), { onSuccess: () => form.reset() })
</script>

<template>
  <form @submit.prevent="submit">
    <input v-model="form.title" placeholder="What needs doing?" />
    <button type="submit" :disabled="form.processing">Add</button>
    <div v-if="form.errors.title" style="color: crimson">{{ form.errors.title }}</div>
  </form>
</template>
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
  import { useForm } from '@inertiajs/svelte'
  import { routes } from '../../types/routes'

  const form = useForm({ title: '' })
  const submit = (e: SubmitEvent) => {
    e.preventDefault()
    form.submit(routes.todos.store(), { onSuccess: () => form.reset() })
  }
</script>

<form onsubmit={submit}>
  <input placeholder="What needs doing?" bind:value={form.title} />
  <button type="submit" disabled={form.processing}>Add</button>
  {#if form.errors.title}
    <div style="color: crimson">{form.errors.title}</div>
  {/if}
</form>
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## 4. Try the development tools

**Follow the route in your editor.** Jump to the definition of `routes.todos.store()`. The starter generates `ClientApp/types/routes.ts` from your named C# endpoints. That function supplies both the URL and the HTTP method to the form.

**Explore the data your page receives.** Find `InertiaPages['Todos/Index']` in the page component. To see the type, hover over `todos` in your editor or open `ClientApp/types/inertia.d.ts`. The starter generates that declaration from the C# `TodosPage` record in `Program.cs`.

**Inspect a submission in your browser.** The starter already records visits in Development. Open the Inertia panel and submit an empty title again. Then inspect the request and the page data that contains the error. [Install the browser extension and open the panel](/docs/devtools#try-it-in-the-starter)

## Next steps

- [Test a form submission](/docs/testing#testing-a-form-with-antiforgery) to check the validation error in a .NET test.
- [Add Inertia to an existing ASP.NET Core app](/docs/quick-start) to bring the same workflow to your own project.

# Installation

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/installation

> Install Inertia.Net, the optional MVC, FastEndpoints, SignalR, Redis or MongoDB package, and the testing helpers.

Inertia.Net is split into small packages. Install the core package and one optional backend integration.

| Package | Install when |
|---|---|
| `Inertia.Net` | always. The core adapter, Minimal API support, Vite, server-side rendering (SSR), state store and antiforgery |
| `Inertia.Net.Mvc` | you use MVC controllers: `ModelState` filter, Razor root view and tag helpers |
| `Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints` | you use FastEndpoints: `Send` extensions, validation pre-processor and Precognition |
| `Inertia.Net.Live.SignalR` | you deliver [live props](/docs/live-props) over SignalR: hub, channel authorization and broadcaster |
| `Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore` | you page EF Core queries with numbered or cursor pagination |
| `Inertia.Net.Redis` | you share [cached props](/docs/props#cached-props) and SSR renders between app instances through Redis |
| `Inertia.Net.MongoDB` | you page MongoDB finds with numbered or cursor [pagination](/docs/pagination#with-mongodb) |
| `Inertia.Net.Testing` | in your test project: fluent assertions over Inertia responses |
| `Inertia.Net.Templates` | you want to start from a complete app. Install it with `dotnet new install Inertia.Net.Templates` |

```sh
dotnet add package Inertia.Net --version 1.9.8
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.Mvc --version 1.9.8            # MVC only
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints --version 1.9.8  # FastEndpoints only
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore --version 1.9.8 # EF Core pagination
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.Testing --version 1.9.8        # test projects
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.Live.SignalR --version 1.9.8   # live props over SignalR
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.Redis --version 1.9.8          # Redis cache store
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.MongoDB --version 1.9.8        # MongoDB pagination
```

Use the same version for every Inertia.Net package. The package version and the Inertia.js protocol version are separate numbers: Inertia.Net 1.9.8 implements Inertia.js v3.

## Requirements

- .NET 10 or .NET 11 SDK and a `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` project.
- JavaScript frontend build tools with npm, Bun, pnpm or Yarn. Managed SSR requires Node.js or Bun at runtime.
- An Inertia.js v3 client: `@inertiajs/react`, `@inertiajs/vue3` or `@inertiajs/svelte`.

## .NET 10 and .NET 11

Every package ships `net10.0` and `net11.0` assemblies. NuGet picks the one that matches your app. On .NET 11, keep these points in mind:

- **Use 1.8.0 or later on .NET 11.** Inertia.Net 1.7.1 and earlier were built against .NET 10 only. .NET 11 changed the experimental resolver API of `Microsoft.Extensions.Validation`. Because of that change, `WithInertiaValidation()` and `WithInertiaPrecognition()` from 1.7.1 fail on .NET 11 with `TypeLoadException: Could not load type 'Microsoft.Extensions.Validation.IValidatableInfo'`.
- **Retarget, don't roll forward.** A `net10.0` app that calls `AddValidation()` fails when it runs on the .NET 11 runtime (`DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=LatestMajor`). It fails whatever adapter it uses, because the validation source generator wrote .NET 10 types that .NET 11 removed. To fix it, set `<TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework>` and rebuild.
- **Dependencies follow the target framework.** On `net11.0`, `Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore` depends on EF Core 11 and `Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints` depends on FastEndpoints 9. On `net10.0` they use EF Core 10.0.15 and FastEndpoints 8.3.0. Reference the `FastEndpoints.Generator` version that matches your FastEndpoints version.
- **Async validators.** Errors from `AsyncValidationAttribute` and `IAsyncValidatableObject` go through `WithInertiaValidation()` and `WithInertiaPrecognition()` in the same way as synchronous errors. See [Validation and errors](/docs/validation-and-errors).
- **Automatic CSRF check.** Apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` also get the framework's `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Origin` check. `UseInertiaAntiforgery()` is still the token check Inertia needs. See [CSRF and antiforgery](/docs/csrf-and-antiforgery).
- **C# 15 unions** work as props and in the generated TypeScript. See [Props](/docs/props) and [TypeScript](/docs/typescript).
- **Compression.** `AddResponseCompression()` also offers Zstandard and always adds `Vary: Accept-Encoding`. Inertia's `Vary: X-Inertia` stays next to it.

## Start from the template

```sh
dotnet new install Inertia.Net.Templates@1.9.8
dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react
cd MyApp
```

For another client, choose `--framework vue` or `--framework svelte`. For cookie sign-in, add `--auth` (see [Authentication](/docs/authentication)). The template includes working pages, a Todos form, validation, flash messages, CSRF protection and Vite configuration. The template's client has `lint` (oxlint), `format` and `format:check` (oxfmt) scripts. The `build` script type-checks first. Outside Development the app redirects to HTTPS and sends HSTS. The app targets .NET 10 (LTS) by default. To target .NET 11, add `--tfm net11.0`.

Install dependencies, then start Vite. Use the package manager you chose for your app. All four are supported:

| Package manager | Install dependencies | Start Vite | Build assets |
|---|---|---|---|
| npm | `npm install` | `npm run dev` | `npm run build` |
| Bun | `bun install` | `bun run dev` | `bun run build` |
| pnpm | `pnpm install` | `pnpm run dev` | `pnpm run build` |
| Yarn | `yarn install` | `yarn run dev` | `yarn run build` |

Keep Vite running and start ASP.NET Core in another terminal with `dotnet watch`. For production, run the build command from your
row of the table, then run `dotnet publish -c Release`. Keep the lockfile for the package manager you choose.

## Namespace and global usings

The namespace is `Inertia.Net` and the static factory class is `Inertia.Net.Inertia`. C# resolves a leading `Inertia` to the namespace, so `Inertia.Render(...)` does not compile outside the `Inertia.Net` namespace.

The package's `buildTransitive` props file adds both global usings below when `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>` is set. That setting is the default in new projects.

```csharp
global using Inertia.Net;
global using static Inertia.Net.Inertia;
```

With these usings, you write `Render(...)`, `Defer(...)`, `Once(...)`, `Back()` and `Location(...)` without a namespace or class prefix.

<Callout type="warning" title="Opting out">
Set `<InertiaNetImplicitUsings>false</InertiaNetImplicitUsings>` and add `using static Inertia.Net.Inertia;` yourself, or call `Inertia.Net.Inertia.Render(...)`. `HttpContext.Inertia()` is an extension method and works as written.
</Callout>

## Next steps

<Cards>
  <Card title="Quick start" icon="rocket" href="/docs/quick-start">
    Add the four pieces every Inertia app needs: services, middleware, a root template and a client.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Client setup" icon="code" href="/docs/client-setup">
    Install React, Vue or Svelte and configure Vite for development and production.
  </Card>
</Cards>

# Client setup

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/client-setup

> Configure Vite and the React, Vue or Svelte client for an Inertia.Net app.

Inertia.Net uses the Inertia.js v3 protocol. Install a v3 client package. Inertia.Net does not support v2 clients.

## Install the client

Run the client setup commands from the ASP.NET Core project directory, the one that contains your `.csproj`. You can use npm, Bun,
pnpm or Yarn. The framework snippets below use npm commands. For another package manager, replace each command with its equivalent:

| Package manager | Add packages | Add development packages |
|---|---|---|
| npm | `npm install <packages>` | `npm install -D <packages>` |
| Bun | `bun add <packages>` | `bun add -D <packages>` |
| pnpm | `pnpm add <packages>` | `pnpm add -D <packages>` |
| Yarn | `yarn add <packages>` | `yarn add -D <packages>` |

Replace `<packages>` with the names and version ranges from your framework's snippet. If the project has no `package.json`,
create one first with `npm init -y`, `bun init -y`, `pnpm init` or `yarn init`.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```sh
npm install react react-dom @vitejs/plugin-react @inertiajs/react@^3
npm install -D vite typescript @types/node @types/react @types/react-dom
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```sh
npm install vue @vitejs/plugin-vue @inertiajs/vue3@^3
npm install -D vite typescript @types/node
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```sh
npm install svelte @sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte @inertiajs/svelte@^3
npm install -D vite typescript @types/node
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

`@types/node` provides the types for the `node:fs` import and for `process` in the Vite config. Add `vite/client` to `tsconfig.json` so that `import.meta.glob` is typed:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["vite/client", "node"]
  },
  "include": ["resources/js", "vite.config.ts"]
}
```

For Vue and Svelte, use `"jsx": "preserve"` or omit that setting.

The starter templates use `ClientApp/pages`. The manual examples below use `resources/js/Pages`. Keep the resolver, file paths and Vite entry consistent with the layout you choose.

The templates also ship `ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts`, the client transport for [live props over SignalR](/docs/live-props#signalr). To turn the transport on, uncomment `live: signalr()` in `ClientApp/app.tsx` (or `app.ts`).

## Vite configuration

The Vite config is the same for every client, except for the framework plugin and the entry file. The entry file is `app.tsx` for React and `app.ts` for Vue and Svelte.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig, type Plugin } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import { mkdirSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs'

// Writes the dev server URL to wwwroot/hot. Inertia.Net reads it in Development
// and renders the dev-server tags instead of the manifest tags.
function hotFile(): Plugin {
  const file = 'wwwroot/hot'
  return {
    name: 'inertia-net-hot-file',
    apply: 'serve',
    configureServer(server) {
      server.httpServer?.once('listening', () => {
        const address = server.httpServer!.address()
        if (address && typeof address === 'object') {
          mkdirSync('wwwroot', { recursive: true })
          writeFileSync(file, `http://localhost:${address.port}`)
        }
      })
      const clean = () => rmSync(file, { force: true })
      process.on('exit', clean)
      process.on('SIGINT', () => process.exit())
      process.on('SIGTERM', () => process.exit())
    },
  }
}

export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  plugins: [react(), hotFile()],
  // Built assets live at /build/. The dev server serves from the root because
  // Inertia.Net emits {origin}/@vite/client and {origin}/{entry}.
  base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/',
  server: { port: 5173, strictPort: true, origin: 'http://localhost:5173' },
  build: {
    outDir: 'wwwroot/build',
    emptyOutDir: true,
    manifest: true,
    rollupOptions: { input: 'resources/js/app.tsx' },
  },
}))
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig, type Plugin } from 'vite'
import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue'
import { mkdirSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs'

// Writes the dev server URL to wwwroot/hot. Inertia.Net reads it in Development
// and renders the dev-server tags instead of the manifest tags.
function hotFile(): Plugin {
  const file = 'wwwroot/hot'
  return {
    name: 'inertia-net-hot-file',
    apply: 'serve',
    configureServer(server) {
      server.httpServer?.once('listening', () => {
        const address = server.httpServer!.address()
        if (address && typeof address === 'object') {
          mkdirSync('wwwroot', { recursive: true })
          writeFileSync(file, `http://localhost:${address.port}`)
        }
      })
      const clean = () => rmSync(file, { force: true })
      process.on('exit', clean)
      process.on('SIGINT', () => process.exit())
      process.on('SIGTERM', () => process.exit())
    },
  }
}

export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  plugins: [vue(), hotFile()],
  // Built assets live at /build/. The dev server serves from the root because
  // Inertia.Net emits {origin}/@vite/client and {origin}/{entry}.
  base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/',
  server: { port: 5173, strictPort: true, origin: 'http://localhost:5173' },
  build: {
    outDir: 'wwwroot/build',
    emptyOutDir: true,
    manifest: true,
    rollupOptions: { input: 'resources/js/app.ts' },
  },
}))
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig, type Plugin } from 'vite'
import { svelte } from '@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte'
import { mkdirSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs'

// Writes the dev server URL to wwwroot/hot. Inertia.Net reads it in Development
// and renders the dev-server tags instead of the manifest tags.
function hotFile(): Plugin {
  const file = 'wwwroot/hot'
  return {
    name: 'inertia-net-hot-file',
    apply: 'serve',
    configureServer(server) {
      server.httpServer?.once('listening', () => {
        const address = server.httpServer!.address()
        if (address && typeof address === 'object') {
          mkdirSync('wwwroot', { recursive: true })
          writeFileSync(file, `http://localhost:${address.port}`)
        }
      })
      const clean = () => rmSync(file, { force: true })
      process.on('exit', clean)
      process.on('SIGINT', () => process.exit())
      process.on('SIGTERM', () => process.exit())
    },
  }
}

export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  plugins: [svelte(), hotFile()],
  // Built assets live at /build/. The dev server serves from the root because
  // Inertia.Net emits {origin}/@vite/client and {origin}/{entry}.
  base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/',
  server: { port: 5173, strictPort: true, origin: 'http://localhost:5173' },
  build: {
    outDir: 'wwwroot/build',
    emptyOutDir: true,
    manifest: true,
    rollupOptions: { input: 'resources/js/app.ts' },
  },
}))
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Add these fields to `package.json`:

```json
{ "type": "module", "scripts": { "dev": "vite", "build": "vite build" } }
```

Pass the manifest key of the entry to `@vite("...")`. The key is `resources/js/app.tsx` for React and `resources/js/app.ts` for Vue and Svelte.

## Client entry

The optional `@inertiajs/vite` plugin resolves pages and mounts the app for you. With the plugin, the client entry file needs only this:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```ts
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'

createInertiaApp()
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```ts
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/vue3'

createInertiaApp()
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```ts
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/svelte'

createInertiaApp()
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Without the plugin, you provide the resolver and the setup function yourself.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
// resources/js/app.tsx
import { createInertiaApp, type ResolvedComponent } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob<{ default: ResolvedComponent }>('./Pages/**/*.tsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.tsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    if (!el) throw new Error('Inertia root element not found')
    createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
  },
})
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```ts
// resources/js/app.ts
import { createApp, h, type DefineComponent } from 'vue'
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/vue3'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob<{ default: DefineComponent }>('./Pages/**/*.vue', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.vue`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props, plugin }) {
    if (!el) throw new Error('Inertia root element not found')
    createApp({ render: () => h(App, props) }).use(plugin).mount(el)
  },
})
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```ts
// resources/js/app.ts
import { mount } from 'svelte'
import { createInertiaApp, type ResolvedComponent } from '@inertiajs/svelte'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob<ResolvedComponent>('./Pages/**/*.svelte', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.svelte`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    if (!el) throw new Error('Inertia root element not found')
    mount(App, { target: el, props })
  },
})
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Pages

A page file receives the props from `Render(...)` as normal component props.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
// resources/js/Pages/Users/Index.tsx
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/react'

export default function Index({ users }: { users: { id: number; name: string }[] }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map((u) => (
        <li key={u.id}><Link href={`/users/${u.id}`}>{u.name}</Link></li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```vue
<!-- resources/js/Pages/Users/Index.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Link } from '@inertiajs/vue3'
defineProps<{ users: { id: number; name: string }[] }>()
</script>

<template>
  <ul><li v-for="u in users" :key="u.id"><Link :href="`/users/${u.id}`">{{ u.name }}</Link></li></ul>
</template>
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```svelte
<!-- resources/js/Pages/Users/Index.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">
  import { Link } from '@inertiajs/svelte'
  let { users }: { users: { id: number; name: string }[] } = $props()
</script>

<ul>{#each users as u (u.id)}<li><Link href={`/users/${u.id}`}>{u.name}</Link></li>{/each}</ul>
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout type="tip" title="Use the generated types">
Inertia.Net can write TypeScript declarations for your page props, shared props and flash data. See [TypeScript types](/docs/typescript).
</Callout>

## Development workflow

Run Vite in one terminal and the app in a second terminal:

```sh
npm run dev          # or bun/pnpm/yarn run dev; Vite writes wwwroot/hot
dotnet watch         # terminal 2: the app, ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development
```

Open the ASP.NET Core URL, not the Vite URL. Two servers run side by side:

| URL | What it is | Open it? |
|---|---|---|
| `http://localhost:5180` (the template's default) | Your app. ASP.NET Core routes the request, runs your endpoint and renders the Inertia page. | Yes |
| `http://localhost:5173` | The Vite dev server. It only serves JavaScript, CSS and hot-reload updates to the page above. | No. It has no pages, so it shows a blank page. |

Vite prints `localhost:5173` prominently when it starts. That address is for the browser's asset requests, not for you to open. In Development the app reads `wwwroot/hot` and renders the Vite tags. In production the app reads the manifest.

For production:

```sh
npm run build        # or bun/pnpm/yarn run build
dotnet publish -c Release
```

You need Node to build the assets. At runtime, you need Node only when server-side rendering (SSR) is enabled.

## Using @inertiajs/vite

The `@inertiajs/vite` plugin also provides the SSR dev endpoint and page resolution. In `vite.config.ts`, add it before the hot-file plugin:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```ts
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import inertia from '@inertiajs/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    inertia({ ssr: { entry: 'resources/js/ssr.tsx', host: '127.0.0.1', port: 13714 } }),
    hotFile(),
  ],
})
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```ts
import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue'
import inertia from '@inertiajs/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    vue(),
    inertia({ ssr: { entry: 'resources/js/ssr.ts', host: '127.0.0.1', port: 13714 } }),
    hotFile(),
  ],
})
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```ts
import { svelte } from '@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte'
import inertia from '@inertiajs/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    svelte(),
    inertia({ ssr: { entry: 'resources/js/ssr.ts', host: '127.0.0.1', port: 13714 } }),
    hotFile(),
  ],
})
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

Keep the SSR listener on the loopback address (`127.0.0.1`). The renderer trusts its output and has no authentication. The [SSR guide](/docs/server-side-rendering) covers the full setup.

---

# Quick start

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/quick-start

> Add Inertia.Net to an ASP.NET Core app, create the root template and render your first page.

Use this guide to add Inertia to an existing ASP.NET Core app. To create a new app with the server and frontend already connected, follow [First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes).

Run these commands from the folder of your existing server project. Every app needs the core package:

```sh
dotnet add package Inertia.Net --version 1.9.8
```

For MVC, also install `Inertia.Net.Mvc`. For FastEndpoints, install `Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints`.
Use version `1.9.8` for each. You also need Node.js and Vite to build the client. See
[installation](/docs/installation) for all packages, or [client setup](/docs/client-setup) for the frontend files.

The **root template** is your HTML shell. A **page component** is the React, Vue or Svelte file that renders a screen.
**Props** are the named values your C# handler passes to that component.

Every app needs the same four things:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Register Inertia and the protocol middleware" />
  <Step title="Add a root template with the Inertia tokens" />
  <Step title="Render a page from an endpoint" />
  <Step title="Connect a client and run Vite" />
</Steps>

## 1. Register the services

Choose one backend style. All three use the same protocol middleware and the same `Render(...)` result.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="Minimal API">

```csharp
// Program.cs
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddValidation();                    // .NET 10 source-generated validation
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o => o.HeaderName = InertiaHeaders.XsrfToken);
builder.Services.AddInertia(o =>
{
    o.Share("appName", "Demo");
    o.Pages.Directory = "ClientApp/pages";
});

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles();                                // serves wwwroot/build (Vite output)
app.UseInertia();                                    // before the endpoints
app.UseInertiaAntiforgery();                         // XSRF-TOKEN cookie; 419 for unsafe requests without it

app.MapGet("/", () => Render("Home", new InertiaProps
{
    ["greeting"] = "Hello from .NET",
}));

app.Run();
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="MVC">

```csharp
// Program.cs
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddInertia();
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews().AddInertiaMvc();   // add .UseRazorRootView() here if you want Razor
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o => o.HeaderName = InertiaHeaders.XsrfToken);

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles();
app.UseInertia();
app.UseInertiaAntiforgery();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
```

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

public sealed class HomeController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet("/")]
    public IResult Index() => Render("Home", new InertiaProps
    {
        ["greeting"] = "Hello from .NET",
    });
}
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="FastEndpoints">

```csharp
// Program.cs
using FastEndpoints;
using Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddInertia();
builder.Services.AddFastEndpoints();
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery(o => o.HeaderName = InertiaHeaders.XsrfToken);

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles();
app.UseInertia();
app.UseInertiaAntiforgery();
app.UseFastEndpoints(c => c.ConfigureInertia());           // validation redirect + Precognition
app.Run();
```

```csharp
using FastEndpoints;
using Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints;

public sealed class HomeEndpoint : EndpointWithoutRequest<InertiaResult>
{
    public override void Configure() => Get("/");

    public override Task<InertiaResult> ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct) =>
        Task.FromResult(Render("Home", new InertiaProps { ["greeting"] = "Hello from .NET" }));
}
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout type="tip" title="Why AddValidation and antiforgery up front?">
`AddValidation()` enables the Minimal API integration used by `.WithInertiaValidation()`. `UseInertiaAntiforgery()` issues the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie and validates every unsafe request. This means forms work from the start.
</Callout>

See [Precognition](/docs/precognition) for live form validation.

## 2. Add the root template

The root template is an HTML file in the content root. The default name is `app.html`.

```html
<!-- app.html -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>My app</title>
  @inertiaHead
  @viteReactRefresh
  @vite("ClientApp/app.tsx")
</head>
<body>
  @inertia
</body>
</html>
```

For Vue and Svelte, remove `@viteReactRefresh` and point `@vite` at `ClientApp/app.ts`. The `@inertia` token is required. [Pages and responses](/docs/pages-and-responses#the-root-template) describes the other tokens.

Make sure the build copies `app.html` to the output directory and the publish directory:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <Content Include="app.html" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" CopyToPublishDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
</ItemGroup>
```

## 3. Create the page component

The page name you pass to `Render` must match the client resolver, which finds the page component for a name. With `@inertiajs/vite`, the resolver maps `ClientApp/pages/**` automatically.

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
// ClientApp/pages/Home.tsx
export default function Home({ greeting }: { greeting: string }) {
  return <h1>{greeting}</h1>
}
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```vue
<!-- ClientApp/pages/Home.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
defineProps<{ greeting: string }>()
</script>

<template>
  <h1>{{ greeting }}</h1>
</template>
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```svelte
<!-- ClientApp/pages/Home.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">
  let { greeting }: { greeting: string } = $props()
</script>

<h1>{greeting}</h1>
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

The client entry only needs to start Inertia:

<Tabs>
  <Tab label="React">

```tsx
// ClientApp/app.tsx
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'

createInertiaApp()
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Vue">

```ts
// ClientApp/app.ts
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/vue3'

createInertiaApp()
```

  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Svelte">

```ts
// ClientApp/app.ts
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/svelte'

createInertiaApp()
```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout type="info" title="Not using @inertiajs/vite?">
Pass your own `resolve` and `setup` functions to `createInertiaApp`. The [client setup](/docs/client-setup) page shows both forms for React, Vue and Svelte.
</Callout>

## 4. Run it

If your app has no Vite setup yet, follow the package and configuration steps in [Client setup](/docs/client-setup#install-the-client). Use `ClientApp/app.tsx` (React) or `ClientApp/app.ts` (Vue and Svelte) as the Vite entry to match the root template above.

For the `createInertiaApp()` examples above, add `@inertiajs/vite@^3` as a development dependency. In `vite.config.ts`, import `inertia` from `@inertiajs/vite` and add `inertia()` after your framework plugin in the `plugins` array. The `inertia()` plugin resolves the page files under `ClientApp/pages`.

From the project directory, install dependencies and start Vite with your package manager:

| Package manager | Install dependencies | Start Vite | Build assets |
|---|---|---|---|
| npm | `npm install` | `npm run dev` | `npm run build` |
| Bun | `bun install` | `bun run dev` | `bun run build` |
| pnpm | `pnpm install` | `pnpm run dev` | `pnpm run build` |
| Yarn | `yarn install` | `yarn run dev` | `yarn run build` |

Keep Vite running in terminal 1. Start ASP.NET Core in terminal 2:

```sh
dotnet watch     # Development environment
```

Open the URL that `dotnet watch` prints, not the Vite URL. The first visit to `/` should display “Hello from .NET”.

For production, run the build command from your row of the table, then publish the app:

```sh
dotnet publish -c Release
```

Deploy `wwwroot/build` and `app.html` with the published app.

## Where to go next

<Cards>
  <Card title="Client setup" icon="code" href="/docs/client-setup">Vite configuration and the React, Vue and Svelte entries.</Card>
  <Card title="Props" icon="blocks" href="/docs/props">Lazy, deferred, merged and cached page data.</Card>
  <Card title="Validation" icon="shield" href="/docs/validation-and-errors">Redirects, error bags and Precognition.</Card>
  <Card title="Server-side rendering" icon="rocket" href="/docs/server-side-rendering">Render the first visit on Node.</Card>
</Cards>

# AI agents

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/ai-agents

> Give coding agents the context and conventions they need to build Inertia.Net pages correctly.

An Inertia.Net app is a good fit for coding agents:

- The backend and the frontend live in one project.
- A feature follows one request path: endpoint, props, page component.
- There is no API contract or client router for the agent to keep in sync.

The main thing an agent needs is to know the conventions. This page gives you that context in a form you can paste into your project.

## Choose the right reference

- **Building an app?** Start with [First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes), then read the guide for the feature you need.
- **Changing the adapter?** Read the repository's `AGENTS.md`, `docs/protocol.md`, and the README's **For AI agents** section.
  They explain the source files, tests and protocol rules. Do not apply repository-maintenance rules to an unrelated consuming app.
- **Looking for a complete Inertia example?** Use [Kitchen Sink](/docs/kitchen-sink), the official v3 demo. You need to
  translate its Laravel handlers to C#. The client-side Inertia patterns are the reference.

Keep examples honest:

- Name the file being changed.
- Say whether a snippet is a complete file or a fragment.
- Run the checks you report.

Do not guess API names from another server adapter.

## Point the agent at the docs

The documentation is published as plain text for language models:

| URL | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`/llms.txt`](/llms.txt) | An index of every page with a one-line summary, following the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) format. |
| [`/llms-full.txt`](/llms-full.txt) | The whole documentation in one Markdown file. |

Agents that can fetch URLs can read these files directly. For agents that cannot, download `llms-full.txt` into your repository, for example as `docs/inertia-net.md`. Then reference the file from your agent instructions.

## Add an AGENTS.md section

Most coding agents read a project instruction file:

- `AGENTS.md` for Codex and many others
- `CLAUDE.md` for Claude Code
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md` for GitHub Copilot
- `.cursor/rules` for Cursor

Copy this section into your instruction file. Adjust the paths and framework to match your app.

````md
## Inertia.Net

This app uses Inertia.Net (Inertia.js v3 for ASP.NET Core). Docs: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/llms.txt

- Pages are rendered from the server. An endpoint returns `Render("Users/Index", props)`;
  the component lives in `ClientApp/pages/Users/Index.tsx`. Names must match exactly, including case.
- Do not add JSON API endpoints or fetch calls for page data. Pass data as props instead.
  Use Inertia `<Link>`, `router` and `useForm` for navigation and forms, not a client-side router.
- `Render`, `Back`, `Location`, `Defer`, `Optional`, `Always`, `Merge` and `Once` are global usings
  from `Inertia.Net.Inertia`. Write them unqualified.
- Props: use `Defer(ct => ...)` for slow data, `Optional(() => ...)` for data loaded only on
  partial reloads, `Merge(...)` for paginated lists and `Once(...)` for data the client can keep.
- Forms: POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/QUERY endpoints validate with `.WithInertiaValidation()` (Minimal API),
  the MVC filter or `c.ConfigureInertia()` (FastEndpoints), then redirect. On success return a redirect
  or `Back()`. Report custom errors with `Back().WithErrors(...)`. Use `Back().WithFlash(...)` for messages.
- Keep antiforgery on: `app.UseInertiaAntiforgery()` is required for unsafe requests.
- Use typed page props (a record per page) for new pages and register them with
  `o.TypeScript.Page<T>("Component")` so the TypeScript types stay generated, not hand written.
- Test pages with `Inertia.Net.Testing`: `client.InertiaGetAsync(url)` then
  `response.AssertInertiaAsync(page => page.Component(...).Has(...))`.
- Before finishing: `dotnet build`, `dotnet test`, and the client build script (`npm run build`, `bun run build`, `pnpm run build` or `yarn run build`).
  Check that the script includes type checking; `vite build` alone does not. Run the framework's type-check command separately if needed.
````

If you use Vue or Svelte, change the component path and extension.

## Asking for a feature

Agents do better with a request that names both ends of the feature. For example:

> Add a `/projects` page. The endpoint returns `Projects/Index` with a paginated `projects` prop using `Merge` and the `InfiniteScroll` component, and a deferred `stats` prop. Add a create form that posts to `/projects`, validates `CreateProjectInput` with `.WithInertiaValidation()`, and redirects back with a `toast` flash message. Add a test with `Inertia.Net.Testing` for the page component and props.

A request like this tells the agent which [props](/docs/props) to use, how [validation](/docs/validation-and-errors) is wired, and how to check the result with [testing helpers](/docs/testing).

## Let the agent check its own work

Agents are most reliable when they can verify a change. Inertia.Net gives them a few cheap checks:

- **Compile-time types.** With [generated TypeScript types](/docs/typescript), a prop renamed in C# breaks the client build. The client build script (`npm run build`, `bun run build`, `pnpm run build` or `yarn run build`) therefore catches mismatches.
- **Response tests.** `Inertia.Net.Testing` asserts the component name and props without a browser. Ask the agent to add one test per page.
- **Missing components.** In Development, [DevTools checks](/docs/devtools) report a `Render` call whose page component does not exist.

<Callout type="tip" title="Starter template">
`dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react` creates an app with pages, a validated form, flash messages, CSRF and Vite already set up. Starting an agent from the template gives the agent working examples of every convention above.
</Callout>

---

# Learn from Kitchen Sink

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/kitchen-sink

> Explore the official Inertia.js v3 demo, then use the same ideas in ASP.NET Core.

The official Inertia.js v3 sample application is **Kitchen Sink**. It combines a small CRM with pages that show forms,
navigation, deferred data, prefetching, state, layouts and error handling.

- [Open the live demo](https://demo-v3.inertiajs.com)
- [Read the source](https://github.com/inertiajs/demo-v3)
- [Read Inertia's demo guide](https://inertiajs.com/docs/v3/getting-started/demo-application)

Kitchen Sink uses **Laravel and Vue**, not Inertia.Net. Its client-side patterns still apply: the server chooses a page,
passes props, validates forms and redirects after submissions. Replace the Laravel handler with a C# endpoint.

The public demo resets its database every midnight. Use it respectfully and do not enter private information.

## Pick one flow to learn

| Try this in Kitchen Sink | Then read this .NET guide |
|---|---|
| Open a page and follow a link | [Pages and responses](/docs/pages-and-responses) |
| Submit an invalid form | [Validation and errors](/docs/validation-and-errors) |
| Show a message after saving | [Flash data](/docs/flash-data) |
| Load a slow section after the page opens | [Deferred props](/docs/deferred-props) |
| Refresh only one list | [Partial reloads](/docs/partial-reloads) |
| Append another page of results | [Infinite scroll](/docs/infinite-scroll) |
| Show a friendly error page | [Error pages](/docs/error-pages) |

## Translate the server, keep the idea

These are handler fragments, not complete application files:

```php
// Kitchen Sink's server-side pattern (Laravel)
return Inertia::render('Contacts/Index', ['contacts' => $contacts]);
```

```csharp
// The same pattern in an ASP.NET Core handler
return Render("Contacts/Index", new InertiaProps { ["contacts"] = contacts });
```

For a runnable .NET example, use this repository's [sample apps](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/tree/main/samples), or create a starter with
[First 10 minutes](/docs/first-10-minutes). The samples use Minimal APIs with React, MVC with Vue,
and FastEndpoints with Svelte. Kitchen Sink is the upstream learning reference. These samples show the .NET setup.

## Check the whole request, not just the JSON

When you add a feature, check that:

- the first visit works
- a link updates the page without reloading the document
- an invalid form shows errors
- a partial reload sends only the selected props plus always props
- an asset-version change triggers a full reload

These checks catch problems that a JSON snapshot alone can miss.

---

# Pages and responses

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/pages-and-responses

> Render components, use MapInertia, and understand the root template and response status codes.

An Inertia page is a component name plus a set of props, the data that the component receives. The server writes this page object into the response. The client resolves the component and renders it.

## Rendering a page

`Render(component, props)` returns an `InertiaResult`. The component name must match your client-side page resolver exactly, including case.

```csharp
app.MapGet("/users", () => Render("Users/Index", new InertiaProps
{
    ["users"] = db.Users.ToList(),
}));
```

`Render` accepts the props in one of these forms:

- An `InertiaProps`, which is an ordered string-keyed dictionary.
- Any `IDictionary<string, object?>`.
- A typed object whose properties are the props.

Nested `InertiaProps` and dictionaries are walked at any depth.

```csharp
public sealed record UsersPage(List<User> Users, string Title);

app.MapGet("/users", () => Render("Users/Index", new UsersPage(users, "Users")));
```

This is the default style, and the rest of these docs use it. If you want typed props, use a record that implements `IInertiaPage`. The record names its component, so `Render(new UsersPage(...))` needs no component string. The record can also hold its own GET handler. See [Page records](/docs/page-records).

Every page has an `errors` prop. It is an empty object when there are no errors. The key order is `errors`, shared props, then page props.

Every response is one of three things, depending on how the request arrived:

<Flow
  caption="Figure: how the adapter chooses between JSON, HTML and a forced reload."
  height={340}
  nodes={[
    { id: 'req', label: 'Request arrives', sub: 'Render() runs in your handler', x: 95, y: 170, tone: 'muted' },
    { id: 'hdr', label: 'X-Inertia header?', x: 300, y: 170, tone: 'primary', shape: 'decision' },
    { id: 'ver', label: 'Asset version matches?', x: 515, y: 170, tone: 'primary', shape: 'decision' },
    { id: 'json', label: 'JSON page object', sub: 'client swaps the component', x: 650, y: 55, tone: 'success' },
    { id: 'conflict', label: '409 + X-Inertia-Location', sub: 'client does a full reload', x: 650, y: 285, tone: 'warning' },
    { id: 'html', label: 'HTML document', sub: 'root template + data-page', x: 300, y: 290, tone: 'primary' },
  ]}
  edges={[
    { from: 'req', to: 'hdr' },
    { from: 'hdr', to: 'ver', label: 'yes' },
    { from: 'ver', to: 'json', label: 'yes' },
    { from: 'ver', to: 'conflict', label: 'no', dashed: true },
    { from: 'hdr', to: 'html', label: 'no: first visit' },
  ]}
  narrow={{
    height: 500,
    nodes: [
      { id: 'req', label: 'Request arrives', sub: 'Render() in your handler', x: 180, y: 40, tone: 'muted', w: 200 },
      { id: 'hdr', label: 'X-Inertia header?', x: 180, y: 140, tone: 'primary', shape: 'decision', w: 200 },
      { id: 'html', label: 'HTML document', sub: 'template + data-page', x: 85, y: 270, w: 160 },
      { id: 'ver', label: 'Version matches?', x: 270, y: 270, tone: 'primary', shape: 'decision', w: 170 },
      { id: 'json', label: 'JSON page object', sub: 'client swaps it in', x: 95, y: 420, tone: 'success', w: 170 },
      { id: 'conflict', label: '409 + reload', sub: 'X-Inertia-Location', x: 275, y: 420, tone: 'warning', w: 160 },
    ],
    edges: [
      { from: 'req', to: 'hdr' },
      { from: 'hdr', to: 'html', label: 'no: first visit' },
      { from: 'hdr', to: 'ver', label: 'yes' },
      { from: 'ver', to: 'json', label: 'yes' },
      { from: 'ver', to: 'conflict', label: 'no', dashed: true },
    ],
  }}
/>

## Per-response options

`InertiaResult` has methods that change one response without changing the component:

```csharp
return Render("Admin/Home")
    .WithRootView("admin.html")
    .WithViewData("title", "Admin");

return Render("Errors/NotFound").WithStatusCode(404);
```

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| `.WithStatusCode(int)` | Sets the HTTP status of the page response |
| `.WithRootView(string)` | Uses another root template for this response |
| `.WithViewData(key, value)` | Makes a value available to `@viewData("key")` |
| `.WithSsr(SsrMode)` / `.WithoutSsr()` | Overrides the server-side rendering (SSR) mode for this response |
| `.WithSsrCache(duration, staleFor?)` | Reuses a server-rendered response for the same page JSON |

## Pages without a handler

`MapInertia` maps GET and HEAD to a rendered page, like Laravel's `Route::inertia`:

```csharp
app.MapInertia("/about", "About", new InertiaProps
{
    ["team"] = team,
});
```

## The root template

On the first visit the response is an HTML document. Inertia.Net reads `app.html` from the content root. You can change the file with `RootView`. Inertia.Net parses the template once and replaces these tokens:

| Token | Output |
|---|---|
| `@inertia` | Without SSR: the page JSON script and the root element. With SSR: the server-rendered body. **Required.** |
| `@inertiaHead` | The SSR `head` tags joined with newlines. Empty without SSR. |
| `@vite("resources/js/app.tsx")` | Vite tags for one or more comma-separated entries. |
| `@viteReactRefresh` | The React Fast Refresh preamble while the dev server runs. Put it before `@vite`. |
| `@viewData("title")` | An HTML-encoded value passed with `WithViewData`. |
| `@@` | A literal `@`. |

Inertia.Net leaves other `@` characters alone, such as CSS at-rules and e-mail addresses. Token arguments accept single or double quotes.

The page JSON is escaped with `\uXXXX` sequences, so a prop containing `</script>` cannot break out of the script element. An example `app.html`:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>My app</title>
  @inertiaHead
  @viteReactRefresh
  @vite("ClientApp/app.tsx")
</head>
<body>
  @inertia
</body>
</html>
```

`RootElementId` changes both the root element id and the `data-page` value. The default is `app`. The client finds the page script by that id.

<Callout type="warning" title="Copy the template">
Inertia.Net reads `app.html` from disk at runtime. Add `CopyToOutputDirectory` and `CopyToPublishDirectory` so the file is present after `dotnet publish`.
</Callout>

### Razor root view (MVC)

With `Inertia.Net.Mvc`, the first-visit HTML can be a Razor view:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews().AddInertiaMvc(o => o.UseRazorRootView("App"));
```

`"App"` finds `Views/Shared/App.cshtml`. The view receives an `InertiaRootViewContext` model and uses tag helpers:

```cshtml
@model InertiaRootViewContext
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>@ViewData["title"]</title>
    <vite-react-refresh />
    <vite entry="resources/js/app.tsx" />
    <inertia-head />
</head>
<body>
    <inertia />
</body>
</html>
```

```cshtml
@* Views/_ViewImports.cshtml *@
@addTagHelper *, Inertia.Net.Mvc
```

`<vite entry="a.ts, b.css" />` takes comma-separated entries. SSR runs at most once per request, and `<inertia-head />` and `<inertia />` share the result. `WithRootView("Other")` takes Razor view names when the Razor root view is enabled.

### A custom root view

Implement `IInertiaRootView` and register it before `AddInertia`:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IInertiaRootView, MyRootView>();
builder.Services.AddInertia();

public sealed class MyRootView : IInertiaRootView
{
    public async ValueTask RenderAsync(InertiaRootViewContext context)
    {
        var writer = context.HttpContext.Response.BodyWriter;
        writer.Write("<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>"u8);
        context.WriteBody(writer);                   // or context.GetBodyHtml()
        writer.Write("</body></html>"u8);
        await writer.FlushAsync(context.HttpContext.RequestAborted);
    }
}
```

## Page URL and path base

The page object's `url` is the request PathBase, Path and QueryString. If your app runs behind a proxy that rewrites paths, set `o.UrlResolver` to return the URL that the browser sees:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddInertia(o => o.UrlResolver = ctx => ctx.Request.GetEncodedUrl());
```

`Back()` and the Vite asset URLs also respect the path base.

---

# Props

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/props

> Lazy, optional, deferred, merged, once, cached and rescued page data.

Props are the data a page receives. `Render(component, props)` takes an `InertiaProps`, a string-keyed dictionary, or a typed object. Inertia.Net walks nested `InertiaProps` and dictionaries, so you can nest props at any depth.

Every page has an `errors` prop. The keys of a page's props come in this order: `errors`, shared props, then page props.

## Choose how to load data

Start with a plain value. Use a lazy loader when the query should run only if the response needs that prop.
Use `Defer` when the page should open before a slow query finishes. Use `Optional` when the data is needed only on request.
`Once` keeps a value on the client across visits. `Cache` keeps a value on the server. They solve different problems.

## Large integer IDs

JavaScript cannot represent every 64-bit integer exactly. Set `o.PreserveBigIntegers = true` at registration to wrap unsafe
integers as `$bigint` markers. The v3 client reads the markers as `BigInt`. The default is false.
To override that choice for one page, return `Render("Orders/Show", props).PreserveBigIntegers()` or
`.PreserveBigIntegers(false)`. Props and flash use the same setting. This is a handler fragment.

**C# 15 unions (.NET 11).** A prop can have a `union` type, for example `public union Subject(User, Team);`. Inertia.Net writes such a prop as the JSON of its active case, with no wrapper or discriminator, through your source-generated `JsonSerializerContext`. Partial reloads select it like any other prop. Inertia.Net does not resolve an `InertiaProp` (`Defer`, `Optional`, ...) stored inside a union case, so keep lazy props at the page level.

## The prop factories

| C\# | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `["title"] = "Hi"` | A plain value. Sent on every response that includes the key. |
| `Prop(() => ...)` | Lazy: the loader runs only when the prop is part of the response. |
| `Always(value)` or `Always(() => ...)` | Sent even when a partial reload does not ask for it. |
| `Optional(() => ...)` | Never sent on the first visit, only when a partial reload asks for it. |
| `Defer(() => ..., group: "name")` | Left out of the first response. The client loads it right away with its group. |
| `Merge(value)` | The client appends the new value to its current one. |
| `DeepMerge(value)` | The client deep merges the value. |
| `Once(() => ...)` | Resolved once and remembered by the client. |
| `Scroll(page, wrapper: "data", metadata)` | An infinite-scroll prop with paging metadata. |

Every lazy factory (`Prop`, `Always`, `Optional`, `Defer`, `Merge`, `DeepMerge`, `Once`, `Scroll`) accepts five loader shapes:

```csharp
Prop(() => value)                                  // Func<T>
Prop(() => repo.GetAsync())                        // Func<Task<T>>
Prop(() => repo.GetValueTaskAsync())               // Func<ValueTask<T>>
Prop(ct => repo.GetAsync(ct))                      // Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>>
Prop(ct => repo.GetValueTaskAsync(ct))             // Func<CancellationToken, ValueTask<T>>
```

The cancellation token a loader receives is `HttpContext.RequestAborted`. An `async` lambda always binds to the awaiting overload, never to “a prop whose value is a Task”.

Fluent methods mutate and return the same instance: `.Once(key?, until?)`, `.As(key)`, `.Until(ttl)`, `.Fresh()`, `.Append(path?, matchOn?)`, `.Prepend(path?, matchOn?)`, `.DeepMerge()`, `.MatchOn(params keys)`, `.Defer(group)`, `.WithGroup(group)`, `.Rescue()`, `.Parallel()`, `.Cache(key, duration)` and `.Cache(key, duration, staleFor?, tags?)`.

`Fresh()` makes a prop a once prop, and `WithGroup()` makes it deferred. Repeated `MatchOn()` calls add keys. Root `Append()` and `Prepend()` are mutually exclusive, and combining them throws. Fluent methods mutate the prop, so create prop instances per request. Do not share prop instances across requests.

## Resolution order

By default, loaders run one after another, in prop order. A loader runs only when its prop is included in the response. Because loaders run one at a time, a scoped EF Core `DbContext` is safe to use in several loaders.

```csharp
return Render("Users/Index", new InertiaProps
{
    ["title"] = "Users",
    ["users"] = Prop(ct => db.Users.ToListAsync(ct)),
    ["filters"] = Always(new { search = "ann" }),
});
```

```json
{
  "component": "Users/Index",
  "props": { "errors": {}, "title": "Users", "users": [ { "id": 1, "name": "Ann" } ], "filters": { "search": "ann" } },
  "url": "/users?search=ann",
  "version": "3f9a1c0d5b7e2a64c8d1e0f9b3a57c21",
  "sharedProps": ["errors"]
}
```

Inertia.Net buffers the page before sending it, so a loader that throws never produces a half-written `200`.

### Parallel props

Mark independent async loaders with `.Parallel()` to start them together:

```csharp
return Render("Dashboard", new InertiaProps
{
    ["stats"] = Prop(ct => statsService.GetAsync(ct)).Parallel(),
    ["activity"] = Defer(ct => activityService.RecentAsync(ct)).Parallel(),
    ["user"] = currentUser, // values and sync loaders resolve in turn
});
```

- Only `Task` and `ValueTask` loaders can be parallel. `Parallel()` throws for values and synchronous loaders.
- At most `InertiaOptions.Props.MaxConcurrency` loaders run at once per render. The default is 4.
- Top-level props and props inside literal objects (`InertiaProps` and other string-keyed dictionaries) start early. Parallel props anywhere else resolve in turn.
- Loaders of props that are not part of the response never start.
- If a loader fails, Inertia.Net cancels and awaits the others. The render then fails with the first failure in prop order. A `Rescue()`d prop fails alone.

<Callout type="warning" title="DbContext and HttpContext">
A parallel loader must not use the request's `DbContext` or other non-thread-safe scoped services, and must not touch `HttpContext`. Give each loader its own context through `IDbContextFactory<T>` or its own scope.
</Callout>

```csharp
["orders"] = Prop(async ct =>
{
    await using var db = await dbFactory.CreateDbContextAsync(ct);
    return await db.Orders.CountAsync(ct);
}).Parallel(),
```

### Scoped services in loaders

`Prop<TService, T>(...)` hands a loader a service from the request, without capturing it in a closure:

```csharp
["orders"] = Prop<AppDbContext, int>((db, ct) => db.Orders.CountAsync(ct)),
["inbox"] = Prop<InboxService, Inbox>((inbox, ct) => inbox.LoadAsync(ct)).Defer(), // and .Once(), .Cache(...), .Live(...), .Rescue()
```

- A loader that runs during the request gets the request's instance. This is the same `DbContext` the handler used.
- A `.Parallel()` loader gets a scope of its own, so two parallel loaders never share a `DbContext`. The scope is disposed when the loader finishes.
- A [stale-while-revalidate](#cached-props) refresh runs after the response, in a new scope. That scope is disposed when the refresh ends.
- If the service is not registered, the render fails with the prop's path and the service type.

## Deferred props

`Defer` leaves the prop out of the first response and lists it under `deferredProps`. The client asks for each group as soon as the page is mounted.

```csharp
["stats"] = Defer(ct => stats.GetAsync(ct)),                 // group "default"
["feed"]  = Defer(ct => feed.GetAsync(ct), group: "sidebar"),
```

```json
{ "props": { "errors": {} }, "deferredProps": { "default": ["stats"], "sidebar": ["feed"] } }
```

See [Deferred props](/docs/deferred-props) for the client component and the request rules.

## Merge props

```csharp
["posts"]    = Merge(posts),                                  // append
["messages"] = Prop(() => messages).Prepend(),                // prepend
["settings"] = DeepMerge(settings),
["rows"]     = Merge(rows).MatchOn("id"),                     // replace items with the same id
["chat"]     = Merge(chat).Append("messages", matchOn: "id"), // append at a nested path
```

```json
{
  "mergeProps": ["posts", "chat.messages"],
  "prependProps": ["messages"],
  "deepMergeProps": ["settings"],
  "matchPropsOn": ["rows.id", "chat.messages.id"]
}
```

The full behavior is in [Merging props](/docs/merging-props).

## Once props

```csharp
["plans"] = Once(ct => plans.AllAsync(ct)).Until(TimeSpan.FromHours(1)).As("billing-plans"),
```

```json
{
  "props": { "errors": {}, "plans": [ { "id": "pro" } ] },
  "onceProps": { "billing-plans": { "prop": "plans", "expiresAt": 1760000000000 } }
}
```

When the client already holds the key, it sends `X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props`. The value is then left out, and the `onceProps` entry stays. See [Once props](/docs/once-props).

## Cached props

`.Cache(key, duration)` keeps a prop's value as JSON in the cache. The default cache is the app's `IMemoryCache`. A cache hit costs neither the query nor serialization.

```csharp
return Render("Dashboard", new InertiaProps
{
    ["stats"] = Prop(ct => stats.ComputeAsync(ct)).Cache("dashboard-stats", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)),
    ["orders"] = Defer(ct => orders.RecentAsync(userId, ct)).Cache($"orders:{userId}", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), tags: [$"user:{userId}"]),
    ["catalog"] = Optional(() => catalog.All()).Cache("catalog", TimeSpan.FromHours(1), staleFor: TimeSpan.FromHours(23)),
});
```

<Callout type="important" title="The key is the value's identity">
Every request that uses a key gets the same value. Put the user, tenant or anything else the value depends on in the key. Keys live in their own cache space and cannot collide with the app's own entries.
</Callout>

Caching only changes how a prop loads. Optional, deferred, merged, once and scroll props keep their behavior, and their metadata is written from the cache too. A parallel cached prop does not start its loader on a cache hit. A rescued failure is not cached.

**Removing and replacing values.** Inject `IInertiaCache` where the data changes:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/orders", async (OrderInput input, IInertiaCache cache, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    var order = await orders.CreateAsync(input, ct);
    await cache.RemoveByTagAsync($"user:{order.UserId}", ct);
    await cache.RemovePropAsync("dashboard-stats", ct);
    await cache.SetPropAsync("catalog", await catalog.AllAsync(ct), TimeSpan.FromHours(1), cancellationToken: ct);
    return Back();
});
```

`ClearPropsAsync()` removes every cached prop. `ClearSsrAsync()` removes every cached render. `SetPropAsync` serializes the value the way a prop of that type is serialized, and takes the same `staleFor` and `tags`.

The default store keeps cached props in the app's `IMemoryCache`, with no size limit of their own. Set `o.Props.CacheMaxBytes` to cap them. Cached props then go in a private cache, and the least recently used ones are evicted past the cap.

**Stale-while-revalidate.** `staleFor` keeps serving a value after its duration. The first request that reads a stale value gets the stale value at once, and the loader runs after the response has been sent. After `duration + staleFor`, the loader runs during the request again.

- When the response completes, Inertia.Net queues the refreshes on a bounded background worker. The response does not wait for the loader. Loaders that use `staleFor` must use singleton dependencies, or create an independent scope inside the loader with `IServiceScopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope()` or `IDbContextFactory<T>`. Do not capture request-scoped services or `HttpContext`.
- The worker accepts 64 pending refreshes and runs up to 4 at a time. It cancels each refresh after 30 seconds, and cancels all of them on host shutdown. When the queue is full, Inertia.Net drops the refresh and logs a warning. The stale value keeps its existing expiration. Monitor `inertia.cache.refresh.dropped`, tagged with `inertia.cache.kind=prop|ssr`.
- One refresh runs per key and app instance at a time. A refresh that finds the value fresh again skips its loader.
- An `IInertiaCache` removal (`RemovePropAsync`, `RemoveByTagAsync`, `ClearPropsAsync`) can happen while a fill or refresh is running.
