The full table, including workstation GC and RSS after load, is in its job summary and in the [benchmark results](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/blob/main/tests/Inertia.Net.Benchmarks/RESULTS.md). Measure on a quiet machine. On a shared machine, other processes take CPU from both the server and the client, so requests per second varies from run to run.

## Memory and hosting

For capacity planning, the useful number is how much memory the whole process needs at rest and under load, not a microbenchmark. These are reference points for complete apps, measured on Linux x64 after the first request. They are not guarantees:

| App shape | RSS at rest | Peak RSS under load | Plan for |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Inertia.Net JIT app, no database (`samples/MinimalApi.React`) | about 90 MB | not measured | 256–512 MB |
| Inertia.Net Native AOT app (`tests/Inertia.Net.AotSmoke`) | about 42 MB | not measured | 128–256 MB |
| Small JIT todo app: EF Core + SQLite + cookie auth | 115–117 MB | 144–158 MB | 256–512 MB |
| Small Native AOT todo app: `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` + source-generated JSON + cookie auth | 37–39 MB | 50–58 MB | 128–256 MB |
| Managed SSR process, small React app (Bun) | +58 MB | +99–106 MB | add 128 MB |
| Managed SSR process, small React app (Node) | +89 MB | +138–147 MB | add 192 MB |
| Managed SSR process, large app: this docs site, 3 MB bundle (Bun) | +83 MB | +324–344 MB | add 384 MB |
| Managed SSR process, large app: this docs site (Node) | +138 MB | +242–247 MB | add 320 MB |

All rows were measured on Linux x64 after the first request. The rows below the first two come from the [hosting probes](#with-and-without-inertia):

- **Todo apps.** These are the probe's todo mode: a signed-in user's 25 todos, read from SQLite on every request, as an Inertia visit. Both rows cover 64 concurrent connections under server and workstation GC on the GitHub runner. The Native AOT build uses `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` directly, because EF Core's runtime query compilation is not Native AOT compatible.
- **SSR rows.** These are the Bun or Node process that managed SSR starts, measured with `eng/ssr-memory-probe.sh`. The script renders each page once ("at rest"), then sends 3,000 renders from 8 parallel clients ("peak"). The small app is `samples/MinimalApi.React`. The large app is this site's MDX bundle.

A few things to plan for:

- **SSR peaks.** Bun starts smaller, but the large bundle peaked higher under Bun than under Node. Bun handed most of it back within seconds (144–222 MB 3 s later). Node kept its peak (229–239 MB). Size the SSR container for the peak. Runtime flags passed through `n.Arguments` barely change the peak: Bun's `--smol` peaked at 319–322 MB and Node's `--max-old-space-size=128` at 228–230 MB, and both rendered about 2–4× slower. Measure your own bundle with `eng/ssr-memory-probe.sh`.
- **Bigger apps.** PostgreSQL or MongoDB, image processing and a large cache move every number upward, so measure your own app under realistic concurrency.
- **Native AOT.** It removes most JIT and reflection overhead, but it does not make EF Core or a database free.

For containers:

- Set a memory limit for the container instead of relying on the host. .NET uses this limit to size its heap.
- Keep the default server GC with dynamic adaptation (DATAS). DATAS has been on by default since .NET 9. In the hosting probe, turning it off (`DOTNET_GCDynamicAdaptationMode=0`) raised peak memory from 84 MB to 126 MB on JIT and from 47 MB to 122 MB on Native AOT.
- Leave headroom for the GC, the OS page cache and request bursts.
- Expect SSR to add a second process. If the Bun renderer is optional, `SsrMode.Preferred` lets the app fall back to client rendering when the renderer is unavailable.
- Profile with real page sizes. A dashboard with deferred props and a paginated feed behaves very differently from a page that serializes every row.

For in-process render throughput and allocations, use the benchmark project:

```sh
dotnet run -c Release --project tests/Inertia.Net.Benchmarks -- --filter '*'
```

Targeted probes: `--render-probe`, `--ssr-probe`, `--mvc-probe`, `--payload-probe` and `--cache-probe`.

## Make rendering faster: register your JSON context first

Inertia.Net uses System.Text.Json to write props as JSON. If your app has a source-generated `JsonSerializerContext`, register it first in `TypeInfoResolverChain`. Inertia.Net then uses the generated code for plain values (records, lists of records, strings, numbers) instead of System.Text.Json's general-purpose path. In the hosting probe, this reduced CPU work per Inertia request by about 16% on JIT and 20% on Native AOT.

`dotnet new inertia` already does this. In your own app:

```csharp
builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o => o.SerializerOptions.TypeInfoResolverChain.Insert(0, AppJsonContext.Default));

[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web)] // the same settings as ASP.NET Core's JSON options
[JsonSerializable(typeof(TodoDto[]))]
internal sealed partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;
```

Inertia.Net uses the generated code only when the output would be exactly the same. It checks this for you and falls back to System.Text.Json's general-purpose path when:

- the context is not first in `TypeInfoResolverChain`
- its settings differ from your app's JSON options (for example, omitting `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web` gives PascalCase instead of camelCase names)
- your JSON options have custom converters, or `PreserveBigIntegers` is on
- a type has a property name with characters other than letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` and `$`

## Payload size

Inertia.Net builds the whole page in memory before sending the first byte. A loader failure therefore never leaves a half-written `200` response. Each active request keeps its whole page in memory while sending it. The server sends Inertia (JSON) responses in 32 KB pieces, so its send buffers do not hold a second full copy of a large page. Buffers for pages under 1 MB are reused between requests. Larger ones are freed after the response, so one unusually large page does not keep that memory reserved for the life of the app.

Keep pages well under a megabyte:

- paginate with [`Scroll`](/docs/infinite-scroll)
- defer slow data with [`Defer`](/docs/deferred-props)
- load on demand with [`Optional`](/docs/props#the-prop-factories)
- use a [partial reload](/docs/partial-reloads) for refresh buttons and filters

`Ssr.MaxPageBytes` keeps larger pages off the SSR server, and `Ssr.MaxResponseBytes` limits the size of the SSR server's answer. Neither setting limits the props.

## Design notes

- **Single pass.** One recursive walk filters props, runs loaders, writes JSON to a `Utf8JsonWriter` and collects the metadata. There is no intermediate object tree.
- **Pooled buffers.** The page is written to a pooled `IBufferWriter<byte>`, and the path tracker is a pooled `char[]`. A path becomes a string only when metadata needs it.
- **Version check before the handler.** A stale client costs one header comparison and a `409`.
- **No per-request mutable singletons.** Per-request state lives in an `InertiaFeature` on `HttpContext.Features`, so concurrent requests cannot leak history or flash settings into one another.
- **Plain DTOs take the fast path.** Inertia.Net checks whether a POCO, list or typed dictionary can hold `InertiaProp` values (`InertiaProp`, `object` or dictionary members/elements). It caches this result per type and checks the contents for props only for those types. Everything else uses one `Serialize` call, through your [generated JSON context](#make-rendering-faster-register-your-json-context-first) when it writes the same output. An object whose `object` members hold only plain values at render time (no `InertiaProp`, dictionary, `JsonElement` or `JsonNode`) is also serialized in one call, unless a partial reload filters inside it.
- **UTF-8 throughout.** SSR output and the MVC tag helpers write UTF-8 bytes. Nothing large is turned into a .NET string.
- **Cached assets.** The Vite manifest is parsed once, the root template is parsed once into pre-encoded UTF-8 segments, and the production tags are pre-rendered per entry set and path base. The version is a precomputed string compared ordinally. A missing manifest, template or SSR bundle is re-checked at most once per second.
- **Sync loaders stay sync.** `Func<T>` loaders are not wrapped in closures.

Most per-request allocation in a real handler is the props you build, not the render.

## Paired render measurements

Warm, in-process probes on .NET 10 compared 32 alternating rounds in two runs. Times are medians of within-round ratios. B/op (bytes allocated per operation) values are from run 2.

| Workload | Before B/op | After B/op | Run 1 paired time | Run 2 paired time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| JSON, 20 mixed props | 1,736 | 1,736 | −1.6% | −0.6% |
| Integer-key dictionary, 1,000 props | 176,592 | 166,688 | −52.2% | −53.7% |
| GUID-key dictionary, 500 rows | 140,712 | 140,304 | −28.5% | −33.0% |
| Eight scroll props, append wrappers | 6,664 | 6,088 | −2.2% | −3.4% |
| Eight scroll props, prepend wrappers | 6,880 | 6,112 | −6.2% | −5.4% |

These synthetic measurements do not establish HTTP throughput or general latency. Pooled entries grow from 24 to 32 bytes, so warm savings do not imply a smaller cold or concurrent pool footprint. Full methods, controls and rejected candidates are in [benchmark results](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/blob/main/tests/Inertia.Net.Benchmarks/RESULTS.md).

Parallel prop planning and DevTools recording each use a process-wide latch that remains active after first use. Measure with the features used by your own app.

---

# Multiple apps and libraries

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/mounts

> Mount a second Inertia UI under its own path, with its own shared props, asset version, state cookie, root view, error pages and SSR.

One ASP.NET Core app can serve more than one Inertia UI. A typical case is a library, such as an admin dashboard, that ships
its own prebuilt client. A host app that already uses Inertia.Net mounts the library under `/dashboard`.

Each UI is a **mount**: a named `InertiaOptions` that `app.UseInertia(name)` selects inside an `app.Map(...)` branch. The
default mount is the one `AddInertia(...)` and `UseInertia()` configure, so existing apps do not change.

## What a mount keeps to itself

| Per mount | Shared by all mounts |
|---|---|
| Shared props (`o.Share`) and every other `InertiaOptions` setting | `IInertiaCache` and the cache store (choose distinct `InertiaProp.Cache(key)` keys) |
| Asset version: the 409 check only compares against the mount's own version | `IInertiaLive` and the SignalR hub |
| State cookie: `.Inertia.State.{name}` and `.Inertia.Previous.{name}` by default | Metrics (named mounts add an `inertia.mount` tag) and DevTools |
| Root view: the mount's `RootView` file, or a keyed `IInertiaRootView` | Antiforgery and data protection |
| Vite manifest, SSR servers, managed Node processes, TypeScript output | The SSR `HttpClient` (its `ConnectTimeout` comes from the default mount) |
| Error pages registered with `AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...)` | |

## Register and map a mount

```csharp
builder.Services.AddInertia(o => o.Share("user", ctx => ctx.User.Identity?.Name)); // the host app

builder.Services.AddInertia("dashboard", o =>
{
    o.Version = "dashboard-2.1.0";          // the dashboard's own asset version
    o.RootView = "dashboard.html";           // or register a keyed IInertiaRootView, below
    o.Share("product", "Dashboard");
});

var app = builder.Build();

app.Map("/dashboard", dashboard =>
{
    dashboard.UseInertia("dashboard");       // before routing in the branch
    dashboard.UseRouting();
    dashboard.UseEndpoints(e => e.MapGet("/", () => Render("Dashboard/Index")));
});

app.UseInertia();                            // the host app's mount
app.MapGet("/", () => Render("Home"));
```

`Map` sets the request's path base, so these stay inside `/dashboard`:

- page URLs
- `Back()` fallbacks
- Vite asset URLs
- the previous-URL cookie

Calling `AddInertia("dashboard", ...)` again adds to that mount's configuration.

Startup fails when `UseInertia(name)` names a mount that was never registered, or when two mounts share a state or
previous-URL cookie name.

## A root view shipped by a library

A library cannot rely on a file in the host's content root. Instead, register a keyed `IInertiaRootView` that writes an
embedded template:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IInertiaRootView, DashboardRootView>("dashboard");

sealed class DashboardRootView : IInertiaRootView
{
    public async ValueTask RenderAsync(InertiaRootViewContext context)
    {
        var writer = context.HttpContext.Response.BodyWriter;
        writer.Write("<!doctype html><html><head><script type=\"module\" src=\"/dashboard/app.js\"></script></head><body>"u8);
        context.WriteBody(writer); // the page script and root element, written straight to the response
        writer.Write("</body></html>"u8);
        await writer.FlushAsync(context.HttpContext.RequestAborted);
    }
}
```

## Error pages per mount

```csharp
builder.Services.AddInertiaErrorPages();                                         // the host's Error component
builder.Services.AddInertiaErrorPages("dashboard", o => o.Component = "Dashboard/Error");

app.UseInertiaErrorPages();                                                      // once, before the Map branches
```

A mount renders only the error components registered for it, because another mount's components are not in its bundle. A
mount without `AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...)` leaves its errors to the rest of the pipeline.

## SSR, health checks and TypeScript

Each mount has its own SSR gateway. When `o.Ssr.UseNodeProcess()` is set, each mount also has its own managed Node processes.
Give each mount its own `BasePort`. Check a mount's SSR servers with a health check:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks().AddInertiaSsrForMount("dashboard"); // named "inertia-ssr-dashboard"
```

`o.TypeScript.OutputPath` is per mount too, so each client gets its own generated declarations.

## For library authors

Expose one registration call and one mapping call, and keep the mount name private to the library:

```csharp
public static IServiceCollection AddDashboard(this IServiceCollection services) =>
    services.AddInertia("dashboard", o => o.Version = DashboardAssets.Version)
            .AddKeyedSingleton<IInertiaRootView, DashboardRootView>("dashboard");

public static IApplicationBuilder MapDashboard(this IApplicationBuilder app, string path) =>
    app.Map(path, branch =>
    {
        branch.UseInertia("dashboard");
        branch.UseRouting();
        branch.UseEndpoints(e => { /* the dashboard's endpoints */ });
    });
```

Mounts are adapter configuration. The Inertia protocol on the wire does not change.

---

# Redis cache

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/redis

> Share cached props and SSR renders between app instances with the Inertia.Net.Redis cache store.

`Inertia.Net.Redis` keeps [cached props](/docs/props#cached-props) (`.Cache(...)`) and SSR renders in Redis. Every app instance shares them, and a call to `IInertiaCache.RemoveByTagAsync` on one instance clears them for all instances. Inertia.Net reads a page's cached props from Redis together, not one round trip after another. The loaders of those props still run in turn unless you mark them `Parallel()`.

```sh
dotnet add package Inertia.Net.Redis --version 1.9.8
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddInertia();
builder.Services.AddInertiaRedisCache(o =>
{
    o.Configuration = "localhost:6379"; // or leave it unset to use a registered IConnectionMultiplexer
    o.KeyPrefix = "myapp:v1:";          // apps (and cache versions) sharing a server need different prefixes
});
```

The default prefix is `inertia.net:`.

## How entries are stored

- Each entry is a Redis string with the entry's expiration. Each tag is a set of entry keys that lives as long as its longest entry, and each entry keeps an index of its tags.
- Storing or removing an entry is one script. When a removal races a store, the entry ends up either removed, or whole and still tagged.
- Removing a tag works in batches, so a tag on every entry does not block the server.

<Callout type="warning" title="Redis Cluster">
Put a hash tag in the prefix (`{myapp}:`), because an entry, its index and its tag sets change together in one script.
</Callout>

## Failures

Inertia.Net does not hide failures. When the store fails while a page renders, Inertia.Net logs the failure (rate-limited) and renders without the cache. The loaders run, as on a cache miss. `IInertiaCache` calls throw, so a failed invalidation is not silent.

## Native AOT

The Redis store is not verified under [Native AOT](/docs/native-aot).

See the [package README](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/blob/main/src/Inertia.Net.Redis/README.md) and [Deploying behind a proxy](/docs/deploying#multi-instance-state) for the rest of the multi-instance setup.

---

# Framework comparison

URL: https://inertia-dotnet.temtem.dev/docs/framework-comparison

> Compare complete application stacks: ASP.NET Core with Inertia.Net, Next.js, TanStack Start, Nuxt and Laravel with Inertia. Understand their setup, strengths and measured performance.

Choosing a stack starts with the language, backend framework and way of building that suit your team. Speed and hosting cost matter too. To make those trade-offs easier to see, we built the same small app with five application stacks and measured their particular setups side by side.

This page explains what was built, introduces each framework and what it is good at, and then walks through the results in plain terms.

<Callout type="info" title="This is a framework-stack comparison, not an adapter comparison">
The .NET entry is **C# and ASP.NET Core, with Inertia.Net connecting the backend to React pages**. The Laravel entry is PHP and Laravel with Inertia. Next.js, TanStack Start and Nuxt bring their own application structure and rendering tools.

**Inertia.Net does not make .NET faster.** The language, runtime, web framework, database access, rendering and deployment setup all contribute to these results. Inertia.Net provides the page-and-props connection and optional features such as caching. It is not the source of C#'s execution speed or ASP.NET Core's concurrency. These numbers cannot isolate adapter overhead or predict every app's performance.
</Callout>

## What you gain with each setup

| Stack | How you build it | What you gain |
|---|---|---|
| **C# / ASP.NET Core + Inertia.Net** | Keep routing, data access and business logic in .NET. Return React, Vue or Svelte pages and props through Inertia instead of designing a separate page API. | ASP.NET Core's backend tools and .NET's runtime characteristics, plus a modern component frontend. Inertia.Net supplies the connection, not a faster runtime. |
| **TypeScript / Next.js** | Build around React's App Router, server/client components and Next.js data and rendering conventions. | An integrated React application framework, static and server rendering options, and a broad hosting and tooling ecosystem. |
| **TypeScript / TanStack Start** | Use React routes, loaders and server functions with TanStack's typed APIs. | A TypeScript-first workflow with closely connected routing and server calls, and explicit control over data loading. |
| **TypeScript / Nuxt** | Build Vue pages with file-based routing, auto-imports, composables and Nitro server routes. | A cohesive Vue setup with less wiring, modules and integrated server-rendering tools. |
| **PHP / Laravel + Inertia** | Use Laravel routes, controllers and backend services; return component pages through Inertia. | Laravel's conventions and backend ecosystem, with React, Vue or Svelte pages rather than a separately designed page API. |

For example, choosing .NET with Inertia.Net means keeping your C# services and ASP.NET Core infrastructure while adding a component frontend. Choosing Nuxt means adopting its Vue and TypeScript application model. Neither choice is only a different adapter. Each choice changes where your code lives, which tools you use and how you deploy.

## The short version

- **The ASP.NET Core + Inertia.Net setup handled the most traffic in the tests shown**, from first page loads to form posts to heavy calculations. Its Native AOT build also used the least memory and started fastest. These are whole-stack results, not gains caused by installing the adapter.
- **TanStack Start is the leanest JavaScript option.** It used as little memory as Inertia.Net's normal build and started the fastest of all the server-rendered apps.
- **Nuxt's API is very quick**, but its server-rendered pages were slower than the other JavaScript frameworks except Next.js.
- **Next.js and Laravel served the fewest requests** in this setup. Both still answered in a few milliseconds at everyday traffic levels.
- **With caching configured for every stack, the .NET setup was still the fastest in this run**, by 2 to 6 times over the next best on cached first visits. The cache implementations do different work, as explained below.
- **At normal traffic every framework is fast enough.** The differences matter when traffic spikes, when you pay per server, or when a page does heavy work.

## What we built

Each framework runs the same todo app on the same Postgres database and Redis cache:

- **Home page**: a short list of features.
- **Todo list**: 25 or 100 todos from a table of 10,000, newest first.
- **Dashboard**: totals for the whole table, cached in Redis for 60 seconds.
- **New todo form**: checks four fields and saves the todo, or shows one error per field.
- **Heavy page**: a CPU-intensive calculation, run once on one core and once split across all cores.

Each app runs in two modes. In **SSR mode** the server sends a fully rendered page on the first visit. In **SPA mode** the server sends an empty shell and the browser renders it. After the first visit, moving between pages only fetches data, in every framework.

Before any measuring, a parity check confirms that every app returns exactly the same todos, totals, calculation results and error messages. If one app did less work, the parity check would show it.

## The frameworks

<Contenders names={['Inertia.Net', 'Next.js', 'TanStack Start', 'Nuxt', 'Laravel']} />

### ASP.NET Core with Inertia.Net

Inertia.Net lets you write the server in ASP.NET Core and the pages in React, Vue or Svelte, without building a separate API. Controllers or Minimal API handlers return a page name and its data. Inertia's client does the routing in the browser.

**How it was built here**: a Minimal API with React pages, EF Core for the database, `InertiaProp.Cache` for the dashboard, .NET validation with `WithInertiaValidation()`, and antiforgery protection on every form. It ran in two builds:

- **JIT**: the normal .NET build, which optimises itself while it runs.
- **Native AOT**: compiled ahead of time into one small executable. EF Core doesn't support Native AOT yet, so this build reads the database with Npgsql directly. See [Native AOT](/docs/native-aot).

**What comes from .NET and ASP.NET Core**: the C# runtime, concurrent request handling, backend libraries such as EF Core and Identity, and the option of Native AOT.

**What Inertia.Net adds**: returning component pages and props from those endpoints, with Inertia navigation, forms and optional prop/render caching. You keep a .NET backend and a React, Vue or Svelte frontend without building a separate page API. The adapter still does work on each response. It does not make the underlying runtime faster.

### Next.js

Next.js is the most widely used React framework. Its App Router mixes server and client components, and it has its own caching, routing, image handling and a large ecosystem around it.

**How it was built here**: the App Router with server components, Drizzle for the database, zod for validation, and the dashboard cached with `'use cache: remote'` and a Redis cache handler. The form posts to a route handler.

**Strengths**: the biggest React ecosystem and community, React Server Components, static generation and incremental regeneration for content sites, and first-class hosting on Vercel and other platforms.

### TanStack Start

TanStack Start is a newer full-stack React framework built on TanStack Router. It focuses on type-safe routes, type-safe server functions and explicit data loading, and runs on Vite with Nitro as its server.

**How it was built here**: file-based routes with loaders and server functions, Drizzle, zod, and the dashboard cached with Nitro's `defineCachedFunction` stored in Redis.

**Strengths**: end-to-end type safety from route parameters to server calls, a light runtime, very fast startup, and Vite's fast developer experience. It is still young, and its Node server uses Nitro 3, which is a release candidate.

### Nuxt

Nuxt is the main full-stack framework for Vue. It brings file-based pages, auto-imports, data fetching with `useFetch`, and a server layer for APIs, all on Nitro.

**How it was built here**: Vue pages that fetch their data with `useFetch`, API routes on Nitro, Drizzle, zod, and the same Nitro cache in Redis as TanStack Start. Nuxt renders Vue, while the other apps render the same React pages. So part of any difference in page rendering comes from Vue, not from Nuxt itself.

**Strengths**: the most complete Vue experience, conventions that remove a lot of setup, a big module ecosystem, and a fast API layer that can be deployed almost anywhere.

### Laravel

Laravel is PHP's most popular framework. With Inertia, its controllers return React, Vue or Svelte pages the same way Inertia.Net does. In this comparison it runs on Octane with FrankenPHP, which keeps the app in memory between requests instead of starting fresh each time.

**How it was built here**: Eloquent models, a Form Request for validation, `Cache::remember` for the dashboard, and CSRF protection with cookie sessions.

**Strengths**: a developer experience known for being productive, everything built in (auth, queues, mail, scheduling, storage), a huge ecosystem, and the official Inertia adapter, the one Inertia started with.

## The results

To keep labels short, charts and tables call the .NET setup **Inertia.Net** and the PHP setup **Laravel**. Read these as **ASP.NET Core + Inertia.Net** and **Laravel + Inertia**, with the database, frontend and hosting choices described above. They are not measurements of either adapter alone. The JIT and AOT entries also use different database access libraries, so the difference between them does not come only from the compilation mode.

All six apps ran on GitHub's cloud machines. Each test route got its own machine with every app on it, so the apps in any one row of the tables below shared the same hardware. Each app was limited to 2 CPU cores and 2 GB of memory. Every request succeeded, and every server-rendered page really was rendered on the server.

### Memory, startup and image size

Less memory means more apps per server and a smaller hosting bill. Faster startup helps when scaling up under load or running on platforms that start apps on demand.

| App | Memory when idle, SPA / SSR | Startup time, SPA / SSR | Docker image, SPA / SSR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Inertia.Net, Native AOT | **17** / 46 MB | **216** / 514 ms | **34** / 98 MB |
| Inertia.Net, JIT | 27 / 60 MB | 522 / 1,108 ms | 125 / 189 MB |
| TanStack Start | 28 / 29 MB | 263 / **258** ms | 166 MB |
| Next.js | 72 / 76 MB | 715 / 775 ms | 185 MB |
| Nuxt | 138 / 139 MB | 340 / 739 ms | 169 MB |
| Laravel | 98 / 154 MB | 785 / 951 ms | 252 / 311 MB |

In SSR mode the Inertia apps also run a small Node.js process to render pages, which is why their SSR memory is higher. For Laravel the figure includes all its PHP workers.

### First visits

A first visit is what a visitor gets when they open a link or reload the page. In SSR mode the server renders the whole page. This is the todo list with 25 rows:

<Bars
  title="First visits, todo list with 25 rows"
  unit="pages per second"
  data={[
    { label: 'Inertia.Net, Native AOT', value: 3905 },
    { label: 'Inertia.Net, JIT', value: 1764 },
    { label: 'TanStack Start', value: 1294 },
    { label: 'Nuxt', value: 745 },
    { label: 'Next.js', value: 364 },
    { label: 'Laravel', value: 337 },
  ]}
/>

| App | Pages per second | Typical response under full load | Typical response at 50 visits per second |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Inertia.Net, Native AOT | **3,905** | **3.9 ms** | **1.1 ms** |
| Inertia.Net, JIT | 1,764 | 6.6 ms | 1.2 ms |
| TanStack Start | 1,294 | 11.6 ms | 1.4 ms |
| Nuxt | 745 | 19.8 ms | 1.9 ms |
| Next.js | 364 | 41.9 ms | 4.1 ms |
| Laravel | 337 | 32.4 ms | 5.8 ms |

The last column shows what to expect in practice: at everyday traffic, every framework answers in a few milliseconds. The first column is how much traffic one small server can take before it is saturated.

### Moving between pages

After the first visit, clicking a link only fetches the next page's data as JSON. This is what most interactions in an app cost.

| App | Todo list, per second | Dashboard (cached), per second |
|---|---:|---:|
| Inertia.Net, Native AOT | **9,789** | 12,842 |
| Inertia.Net, JIT | 6,155 | **13,465** |
| Nuxt | 5,498 | 10,262 |
| TanStack Start | 3,962 | 7,153 |
| Next.js | 1,512 | 2,283 |
| Laravel | 550 | 1,056 |

Nuxt does well here: its API routes are fast, and on the smallest page it matched Inertia.Net.

### Saving a form

The form test posts a new todo. A valid post is checked and saved to the database. An invalid post fails all four checks and returns the error messages.

| App | Valid posts per second | Invalid posts per second |
|---|---:|---:|
| Inertia.Net, Native AOT | **2,956** | **18,299** |
| Inertia.Net, JIT | 2,810 | 16,314 |
| TanStack Start | 2,464 | 12,559 |
| Nuxt | 1,996 | 11,417 |
| Next.js | 957 | 1,841 |
| Laravel | 517 | 854 |

Saving is limited by the database for every framework, so the fast apps end up close together on valid posts. Invalid posts never touch the database, so they show what the framework itself costs. The Inertia apps also check a forgery-protection token on every post. The JavaScript apps' API routes don't by default.

### Heavy work

The heavy page runs a CPU-intensive calculation. This is mostly a test of the programming language.

<Bars
  title="Heavy work"
  unit="requests per second"
  data={[
    { label: 'Inertia.Net, JIT', value: 1212 },
    { label: 'Inertia.Net, Native AOT', value: 1033 },
    { label: 'Nuxt (cluster)', value: 424 },
    { label: 'TanStack Start (cluster)', value: 389 },
    { label: 'Next.js (cluster)', value: 349 },
    { label: 'Laravel', value: 81 },
  ]}
/>

| App | Requests per second | With 1 / 2 / 4 CPU cores |
|---|---:|---:|
| Inertia.Net, JIT | **1,212** | 648 / 1,260 / 1,938 |
| Inertia.Net, Native AOT | 1,033 | 614 / 1,062 / 1,576 |
| Nuxt (cluster) | 424 | 209 / 408 / 519 |
| TanStack Start (cluster) | 389 | 201 / 389 / 487 |
| Next.js (cluster) | 349 | 179 / 330 / 445 |
| Laravel | 81 | 56 / 79 / 157 |

.NET ran the calculation about three times faster than Node.js and fifteen times faster than PHP. It also used extra cores in one process without any extra code. Laravel gains cores by running more PHP workers.

<Callout type="warning" title="The JavaScript apps get an edge here: cluster mode">
Node.js runs one request's JavaScript at a time, so a single Node.js server uses about one core. To give Next.js, TanStack Start and Nuxt the best chance on heavy work, their numbers here come from cluster mode: one server process per core, sharing one port, as PM2's cluster mode does. Run as a single process, like everywhere else on this page, they handled 207 (Next.js), 227 (TanStack Start) and 240 (Nuxt) requests per second. More cores didn't help. Cluster mode also roughly doubles their memory, since every process loads the whole app. Their cluster numbers come from a [separate run](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/blob/main/benchmarks/frameworks/results/2026-11-17-heavy-work.md) on a different machine.
</Callout>

## Inertia.Net with its caching turned on

All the results above run each setup without page caching. The dashboard data is still cached as described earlier. The results measure the complete request path, not only the framework or adapter. A real app usually caches what it can. So we ran the .NET app once more, next to a copy of itself with Inertia.Net's optional caching features turned on:

- **The SSR render cache** keeps the HTML of a server-rendered page. When the next visitor gets exactly the same page, Inertia.Net sends that HTML without asking Node to render it again. See [Server-side rendering](/docs/server-side-rendering).
- **Two Node renderers** instead of one, so rendering can use both CPU cores.
- **Cached props with stale-while-revalidate**: the dashboard totals and each page of the todo list are kept in memory for a few seconds and refreshed in the background. See [Props](/docs/props).

Plain and tuned builds ran side by side on the same machines:

| Page, first visit | JIT | JIT, tuned | Native AOT | Native AOT, tuned |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Home | 3,528 | **20,800** | 4,378 | 17,952 |
| Todo list, 25 rows | 1,561 | **25,756** | 3,293 | 23,443 |
| Todo list, 100 rows | 562 | **15,119** | 1,033 | 13,745 |
| Dashboard | 2,819 | **20,903** | 3,586 | 18,054 |
| New todo form | 7,068 | **56,746** | 7,773 | 49,923 |

With caching on, server-rendered pages were served 4 to 27 times faster, in about a millisecond, because a cached page skips rendering entirely. Form posts and the heavy calculation didn't change, since nothing there is cached. The second Node renderer adds about 25 MB of memory.

<Callout type="warning" title="Cache what everyone sees the same way">
The render cache uses the page's data as its key, so pages with per-user data make one entry per user. Turn the render cache on for pages that are the same for every visitor, such as landing, catalog and article pages. The other frameworks have caching of their own, so these numbers aren't in the tables above. The next section turns caching on for all of them.
</Callout>

## Every framework with its caching turned on

Comparing a cached Inertia.Net with uncached rivals wouldn't be fair. So we gave every app its own framework's caching, set the same way. Pages are kept for 60 seconds and todo lists for 10. Each is served stale, which means the expired copy is still sent while a fresh copy is made in the background. Everything is kept in the app's memory.

- **Next.js:** `'use cache'` on the page components and their data.
- **TanStack Start and Nuxt:** Nitro route rules, which store the whole response.
- **Laravel:** the popular [spatie/laravel-responsecache](https://github.com/spatie/laravel-responsecache) package, which also stores the whole response.

Requests per second for a first visit, every app with caching on:

| Page, first visit | Inertia.Net | Inertia.Net (AOT) | Nuxt | TanStack Start | Laravel | Next.js |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Home | **55,711** | 50,970 | 18,471 | 12,997 | 1,177 | 558 |
| Todo list, 25 rows | **34,020** | 32,889 | 15,481 | 9,543 | 1,201 | 439 |
| Todo list, 100 rows | **22,834** | 20,007 | 6,835 | 3,882 | 868 | 201 |
| Dashboard | **55,439** | 50,105 | 18,151 | 11,680 | 1,206 | 424 |
| New todo form | **57,611** | 51,266 | 18,603 | 12,129 | 1,180 | 504 |

- **Inertia.Net served 2 to 3 times more than Nuxt and 3 to 6 times more than TanStack Start**, the next fastest. It did so while still running your code and loading fresh page data on every request, which the Nuxt, TanStack Start and Laravel caches skip.
- **Nuxt and TanStack Start gained the most from caching** among the JavaScript frameworks, up to 15 times for Nuxt.
- **Laravel got 2 to 5 times faster** but stopped near 1,200 requests per second, because every request still goes through its session and security layers.
- **Next.js didn't get faster.** Its cache stores the output of components, but a page that reads the address bar, like the todo list, is still turned into HTML on every request. Next.js only serves ready-made HTML for pages that never change per request.

## What Inertia.Net caches, and what it doesn't

Inertia.Net has two caches that work together, and you choose what goes in each.

**The SSR render cache stores HTML, not data.** On a first visit Inertia.Net still runs your endpoint and builds the page's data as usual. It then looks up that exact data. If the same page with the same data was rendered recently, Inertia.Net sends the stored HTML and Node isn't called at all. Rendering with Node is the most expensive step of a server-rendered page, so this is where most of the speed comes from. Because the lookup uses the data itself, the cache can never show an out-of-date page. When one todo changes, the data changes, and the page is rendered fresh.

**Cached props store data.** Add `.Cache(key, duration)` to a prop and Inertia.Net keeps its value, in memory or in Redis. The database isn't asked again until the value expires. With `staleFor`, an expired value is still served while a fresh one loads in the background. This is the only place Inertia.Net will show data that is a little old, and only for the props you mark.

In the benchmark's tuned app, a todo list visit therefore reads the rows from the prop cache, finds the HTML in the render cache, and sends it. All of this takes well under a millisecond on the server. Moving between pages in the browser fetches only data and never involves Node, so for those requests the prop cache does the work.

This is different from the other frameworks' caches, which store the whole response under its address. Those caches skip your code entirely on a hit. But they show the same response, possibly out of date, until it expires. They also need care so that one user's page isn't served to another. Inertia.Net always runs your code, so permissions and per-user data are checked on every request, and you decide which data may be a little old.

See [Server-side rendering](/docs/server-side-rendering) for the render cache and [Props](/docs/props) for cached props.

## What this means for you

- **Pick the framework your team enjoys and knows.** All five are fast enough for most apps at normal traffic.
- **Choose ASP.NET Core with Inertia.Net** if C# and the .NET backend ecosystem suit your team and you want React, Vue or Svelte pages without a separate page API. Treat the measured headroom as a result of this setup, not a speed boost promised by the adapter.
- **Choose Native AOT** for the smallest memory, image and startup time, if plain Npgsql or Dapper-style data access suits you.
- **Choose TanStack Start** for a light, type-safe React stack in TypeScript end to end.
- **Choose Next.js** for the largest React ecosystem, static and incrementally generated content, or Vercel's platform.
- **Choose Nuxt** if your team writes Vue and wants conventions that remove a lot of setup.
- **Choose Laravel** for PHP's most productive ecosystem and everything built in.

<Callout type="info" title="How to read these numbers">
These come from one run on shared cloud machines, with the load generator running next to the apps. Different routes ran on different machines, so compare apps within a table, not one table with another. Measure your own app on your own hardware before you rely on any of them.
</Callout>

## Run it yourself

The app code, the run script and every setting are in [benchmarks/frameworks](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/tree/main/benchmarks/frameworks). Its README explains how to run the comparison on your own machine or on GitHub Actions and lists the caveats. Every route in both modes, with latency percentiles and fixed-rate runs, is in the [full results](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/blob/main/benchmarks/frameworks/results/2026-11-16-v3.md). The run with caching turned on is in its [own results file](https://github.com/adzamkomladev/Inertia.Net/blob/main/benchmarks/frameworks/results/2026-11-16-inertianet-tuned.md).

For what Inertia.Net itself costs next to a plain Minimal API, see [Performance](/docs/performance).
